executive_take:
The signup wall has migrated backwards across the whole category. v0 now builds a complete, self-QA'd site for a logged-out stranger and only then shows a modal ("Create your own app / Sign up to build your idea or duplicate this chat. Free users get $5 in credits per month."). Lovable fires the wall on prompt submit but its docs state it "preserves the prompt through the signup process." GoDaddy's newest builder moved its wall after the prompt while its own legacy Websites+Marketing path still puts it first — the direction of travel is unambiguous. Bolt and Base44 are the laggards: Bolt's own quickstart sequences Build now → sign in → a survey → "approximately five minutes while Bolt creates your app," inserting a questionnaire between intent and payoff.

Remixer is well positioned and under-exploiting it. We already run a live composer with a mic and a Build button on dreamhost.com/remixer, we have the longest no-card window in the category, and we are measurably the fastest to first render: 2–3 minutes against v0's badged "Worked for 6m 21s", Bolt's ~5 min, Base44's 3–5, Wix Harmony's 4–7, Emergent's ~10. Nobody beats us on the clock. But DreamHost's own KB describes the real entry as building "right in the panel," which makes the single highest-leverage question in this lens whether a stranger's landing-page prompt survives DreamHost SSO or gets retyped.

Speed is no longer the wow — anti-slop is. Leaders spend the first expensive seconds deciding taste out loud: Lovable renders three parallel design directions before writing any code; v0 names its direction ("a warm, editorial craft-coffee direction with a deep espresso palette and amber accents") and writes theme colours and font tokens before components; Base44 returns four redesigns side by side; Google AI Studio ships five in one free click. Remixer has no documented equivalent.

Two structural gaps remain. Our free window expires; theirs don't, and they manufacture return visits with a daily credit drip (Lovable 5/day at 00:00 UTC, v0 "$2 of free daily credits on login per user", Framer 500/day, Bolt 300K/day). And we burn credits on publishing — the harshest placement in the field, where Lovable, Bolt and GoDaddy all publish free.

comparison.approach: No wall at all: an anonymous visitor types into the 690x108px composer and gets a complete build, including the agent screenshotting its own output at desktop and mobile widths and fixing a real base-ui defect. Zero pre-generation questions. Signup modal appears only after the build, offering both 'build your idea' and 'duplicate this chat'. Names its art direction out loud and writes theme colours and font tokens before any component. Cost: 6m 21s, and the preview pane reads only 'Your v0 generation will show here.' for the entire wait.
comparison.notes: Best proof-before-ask in the category and the best anti-slop sequencing. Undermined by the slowest first render measured anywhere and a hard cliff from Free ($5 credits, 7 messages/day) to $30/user/mo with no individual plan.

comparison.approach: One ProseMirror composer serves as marketing hero, dashboard entry and editor chat. Wall fires on submit and the prompt is preserved through email/Google/GitHub/Apple auth; user lands in the editor with the build already starting. Zero pre-config — docs are explicit that 'no templates or style pickers exist in this flow'. Typewriter placeholder cross-fades at 500ms teaching verb-first grammar. For visually open-ended prompts it generates three parallel HTML/Tailwind design directions to compare, or runs 'design questions' (font pairs, mood-grouped swatches, wireframe layouts), and skips both for dashboards/admin/URL-clones. Perpetual card-free Free tier with 5 daily build credits.
comparison.notes: The most complete first-run system: one decision to first generation, taste front-loaded, wait made legible by named activity cards and subagent rows, and a daily grant that manufactures a return visit. Free tier is a demo though — read-only code, no custom domain, 30 credits/month cap.

comparison.approach: Prompt-first, wall second: type into the glowing white pill on a violet-black canvas, press 'Start building', then hit GoDaddy SSO. Trust row reads 'Get started for free · 50 AI credits/mo · No credit card required.' Mic is a peer of typing. Eight starter chips under 'Describe your own idea above, or try one of these:' including the switcher hook 'Rebuild my site' and trade-realistic 'Pressure Washing'. No pre-generation questionnaire. Docs actively steer users to free direct editing over paid prompts.
comparison.notes: Strongest entry-screen craft in the field and the right wall placement. Then it falls over: free tier cannot publish at all, credit balance is exiled to a separate Manage-my-plan page (reviewers call it 'a nuisance'), ~8 credits/prompt burns the 50 free in six prompts, and long prompts have hard-failed with a raw 'Bad Request'.

comparison.approach: Free with no card. Prompt box carries an 'I'm Feeling Lucky' button that writes a creative brief for users with no idea, plus AI Chips that attach capabilities (image generation, Maps data) inline. Post-build, one click produces five complete Design Variations — different layouts, colours, typography — previewed and applied without re-prompting. Ships to a free branded name.ai.studio subdomain (10 Jul 2026) and the first two Cloud Run deploys are free, no credit card.
comparison.notes: 'I'm Feeling Lucky' and Design Variations are the two cheapest wow mechanisms found anywhere, and both are free. Weakness is that it is demand-gen for the Gemini API, not a product with retention design — and Google killed Firebase Studio on 19 Mar 2026, which is its own signal.

comparison.approach: Free Starter tier can publish 1 project, including private/password-protected deployments. Prompt box front-loads artifact type via a carousel (Web, Mobile, Slides, Animation, Design, Data Viz, Automation, 3D Game, Document, Spreadsheet) plus a Plan toggle and mic. Agent 3 opens a real browser inside the Agent pane and you watch its own cursor click through the app it just built. Element Editor makes text, font size/weight, alignment, colours, margin and padding edits credit-free.
comparison.notes: The visible self-testing browser is the most legible generation state anyone ships, and free-tier publishing means the first session ends with a URL. Undone by effort-based billing users cannot forecast — The Register documented a customer burning $70 in one night at Agent 3 launch.

comparison.approach: Landing prompt field with placeholder 'Describe the website you want', four quick-start tags plus 'More Ideas', and two actions: 'Refine my prompt' (AI improves the brief before spending) and 'Generate My Site'. Aria then runs a short conversational interview — what the site is about, what to call it, who it's for, desired tone. First usable draft in 4–7 minutes.
comparison.notes: 'Refine my prompt' before generation is a genuinely good pre-flight step nobody in the big five ships. But a 'Don't leave this tab' modal holds the user hostage mid-generation, and reviewers found semantic misfires shipped live — a sustainable clothing brief producing a hero titled 'The Art of Food', and a published 'Shop Now' CTA linked to nothing.

comparison.approach: Hero is a decorative animated composer cycling Build/Send against [Apps][Websites][Games][Tools] — not a working input; every CTA hands off to app.base44.com. Wall fires at prompt submission, framed as work-preservation: 'you will be asked to sign up. This makes sure your work is saved.' Five start paths behind a '+' (prompt, Plan mode, from a URL, from a Figma frame, connect tools). Plan mode interviews on problem, audience, functionality, design preference and key flows at 'a fraction of a credit per message', then 'Start building' costs ~1 credit. 3–5 min to first app.
comparison.notes: Plan mode's cheap-discovery/expensive-execution split is the right economics, and four side-by-side redesign options answer the generic-output complaint. But the fake hero composer wastes the highest-intent moment, and the free tier's 5-credits-per-DAY cap makes a single evening's build session impossible.

comparison.approach: Hero 'What will you build today?' with a dark prompt card, a Plan pill, four 64x88 intent tiles (Website, Slides, App, Prototype) and Figma/GitHub import chips. Then a hard wall: quickstart sequences 'Build now' → 'Sign in or sign up (Google, GitHub, or email: no credit card required)' → complete a survey → 'approximately five minutes while Bolt creates your app.' Nothing renders anonymously. Free tier caps at 300K tokens/day.
comparison.notes: Longest gap between intent and payoff in the category, with a survey deliberately inserted into it. Reviews report the 300K daily cap running out 'before a first build finishes' against Bolt's own five-minute build estimate. The Plan pill offered before the first prompt is the one thing worth taking.

comparison.approach: No standalone funnel at all — entry is hPanel → Websites → 'Add website' → Hostinger Horizons → prompt → 'choose a domain or use a temporary one'. The domain decision is pulled in front of the build. 7-day trial needs no payment info; free plan is 5 AI credits and 1 website. ~5 min to first app. Publish plays a completion sound and offers 'Copy URL' / 'Go to Analytics'.
comparison.notes: The closest structural analogue to Remixer and a cautionary one: burying the builder inside the control panel means there is no acquisition surface, and forcing a domain choice before the user has seen anything is a decision asked at the wrong moment. 5 free credits burn out immediately.

comparison.approach: Live composer with mic and Build button on dreamhost.com/remixer under 'Describe it. Remixer builds it.' and 'Free for 30 days. No credit card required.' Four-step explainer ending 'Preview for Free. Publish When Ready.' Fastest documented first render in the field at 2–3 minutes. No pre-generation questionnaire. Builder shell: dark #18181B, left AI chat ~408px, persistent credits chip in the top toolbar, editable *.remixer.app staging subdomain with a pencil affordance.
comparison.notes: Ahead on clock speed, on card-free trial length, and on keeping the credit balance permanently visible (GoDaddy hides it). Behind on: no documented anti-slop mechanism, no cheap plan/discuss mode, no daily credit rhythm, a trial that expires against perpetual free tiers everywhere else, credits burned by publishing, and an unverified prompt handoff from marketing page into the panel.

best_in_class.why: It is the only product where the entire first-run path is designed as one system rather than a sequence of screens. The composer is literally the same component (data-testid="chat-composer") on the marketing hero, the dashboard and the editor chat, so muscle memory formed before signup transfers intact — the first in-app moment feels already-learned. The wall lands at the highest-commitment instant (submit) and costs nothing because the prompt is carried through auth, so the user lands in the editor with the build already running: one type, one send, one OAuth click to first generation. Nothing is asked before generating — docs are explicit that 'no templates or style pickers exist in this flow' — while the animated typewriter placeholder ('Ask Lovable to create a landing page for my…', cross-fading at 500ms ease-out) quietly teaches verb-first prompt grammar during the hesitation, solving blank-page paralysis with no modal and no tour. The wow is then engineered rather than hoped for: three parallel HTML/Tailwind design directions rendered before any code, capped at six refinements, with an explicit skip list for dashboards, admin tools and URL clones where the user wants speed instead of art direction. The wait is made legible by named activity cards, expandable subagent rows ('Explore: How does the current authentication flow work?') and purpose-built loading keyframes (a literal double-beat heartbeat on the logo) rather than a spinner. And the session has a tomorrow: a perpetual card-free Free tier with 5 daily build credits resetting at 00:00 UTC. v0 beats it on the wall (none at all) and on visible self-QA; Lovable beats v0 on time-to-render, on a live-assembling experience instead of an empty pane for six minutes, and on having any paid step below $30/user/month.

adopt.pattern: Carry the landing-page prompt through DreamHost SSO, and prove it visually
adopt.spec: On submit at dreamhost.com/remixer, POST the prompt to a signed, short-lived draft record and route to SSO with ?draft=<id>. On return, land the user directly in the builder with generation ALREADY running — never in a panel dashboard, never at an empty prompt box. Render their own words as the first message in the left chat panel with a small chip above it reading 'Saved from dreamhost.com — picking up where you left off.' If auth is abandoned, email the draft link 20 minutes later with subject 'Your site is one click from being built' and body opening with their verbatim prompt in quotes. Instrument the funnel as three events: composer_submit → auth_complete → generation_start, and treat any gap between the first and third as the primary conversion leak.
adopt.rationale: DreamHost's own KB says building happens 'right in the panel', which means the marketing composer is at risk of being a decorative on-ramp to a second, empty composer — the exact Base44 failure (animated hero that hands off to app.base44.com). Lovable's docs state the system 'preserves the prompt through the signup process'; that single behaviour is why their funnel is one type, one send, one OAuth click. Retyping is the cheapest possible way to lose a user who has already told you what they want.

adopt.pattern: Rotating typewriter placeholder that teaches DreamHost-audience prompt grammar
adopt.spec: An aria-hidden span beneath the real input, cross-fading with transition-opacity 500ms ease-out, cycling verb-first briefs every ~4s while the field is empty and unfocused. Copy, written for trades and small business rather than SaaS founders: 'Build a booking site for my mobile dog-grooming business in Portland…', 'Build a members area where clients upload photos and pay a deposit…', 'Build a one-page site for my food truck with this week's menu…', 'Rebuild my current site but make it faster and mobile-first…'. Ship the identical composer component — mic, mode pill, send — on the marketing page, in the panel's new-project box, and as the in-builder chat input, so the control the user learns before signup is the control they use after.
adopt.rationale: Lovable's animated placeholder solves blank-page paralysis without a modal, a tooltip or an onboarding tour, and silently trains prompt shape while the user hesitates. Reusing one composer across three contexts is why their marketing page functions as a live demo of the product's primary control rather than a screenshot of it. Both are near-zero cost.

adopt.pattern: Starter chips under the composer, including a switcher hook and a DreamHost-only 'rebuild what I already host'
adopt.spec: Six to eight full-radius pill chips with trailing → arrows, in three ragged centred rows directly beneath the composer, under the line 'Describe your own idea above, or try one of these:'. Contents: Coffee Shop · Landscaping Company · Yoga Studio Booking · Photographer Portfolio · Client Portal with Logins · Rebuild my current site · Rebuild a site I already host here. The last chip is signed-in-only: it reads the account's hosted domains and expands to a domain picker, then pre-fills the prompt from the existing site's headings and copy. Clicking any chip fills the composer with a full sentence (not a keyword) so the user sees the shape of a good brief before pressing Build.
adopt.rationale: GoDaddy's eight chips are lifted almost verbatim from small-trade reality (Pressure Washing, Local Food Truck) and include 'Rebuild my site' as a deliberate competitive-migration hook — a proven pattern from the market leader in exactly our customer segment. The hosted-site variant is available to nobody else: GoDaddy's own 'Rebuild my site' still requires pasting a URL.

adopt.pattern: Three design directions before the expensive build — with an explicit skip list
adopt.spec: After the prompt and before full generation, render three lightweight direction previews side by side, each ~1/3 of the canvas, each with a name and a one-line rationale under it in the format '<Name> — <font pairing>, <palette words>' e.g. 'Warm editorial — Fraunces / Inter, espresso, cream, amber'. Actions per card: 'Use this direction'; global: 'Blend two' and 'Show me three more' (capped at six refinements total). Viewing and choosing costs 0 credits; only the chosen build bills. Skip the step entirely — go straight to building — for app-shaped prompts (dashboards, internal tools, admin panels, 'rebuild this URL') where speed beats art direction. If the full three-direction step is too costly for a 2–3 minute promise, ship the cheaper post-build variant instead: a single 'Try other looks' button that returns five complete alternates (layout, palette, type) to preview and apply in one click.
adopt.rationale: This is now the differentiating wow mechanism, not speed. Lovable generates three parallel directions before writing code and documents the skip rules; Base44's Design Pack returns four options side by side with the promise 'AI shows previews before it touches anything'; Google AI Studio's Design Variations returns five in one free click. Generic AI output is the complaint that kills week-two retention, and re-prompting for aesthetics is simultaneously the most frustrating and most credit-wasteful loop in every metered builder.

adopt.pattern: A cheap, visibly-priced Plan mode offered before the first prompt
adopt.spec: A pill in the composer bottom-right, present on the marketing page AND in the builder, labelled 'Plan · 0.3 credits' next to the default 'Build'. Highlights in Remixer blue #1587FF when active. Toggle with Cmd+. / Ctrl+. and make it work mid-typing so a half-written thought can be reclassified without retyping. In Plan mode the AI asks about audience, key pages, what a visitor should do, and brand feel; the response terminates in quick-action buttons — 'Build this plan', 'Show me an example', 'Change something' — where 'Build this plan' auto-switches back to Build. Never let Plan mode touch the site.
adopt.rationale: Base44 prices Discuss at a flat 0.3 credits against 0.5–4 for execution and explicitly supports Cmd+. mid-typing; Lovable's Plan mode is a flat 1 credit and never touches code; Bolt puts the Plan pill next to 'Build now' on the landing page itself. The pricing asymmetry IS the UX: thinking cheap and predictable, doing metered. It also reduces our own compute spent on doomed generations, and offering it before the first prompt reframes the product from slot machine to collaborator.

adopt.pattern: Make the 2–3 minute wait legible: named design decisions, a queued plan, an elapsed badge
adopt.spec: Left chat streams semantic past-tense rows with an icon, three queued rows shown pre-dimmed and shimmering ahead of execution. Rows must name design decisions in plain language, not file paths: 'Chose a warm editorial direction', 'Set your palette — espresso, cream, amber', 'Paired Fraunces with Inter', 'Mapped out 5 pages', 'Built the hero', 'Wrote your About copy', 'Checked it on mobile'. Interleave one-sentence narration between batches ('Now the pages that use those styles.'). Footer badge on completion: 'Built in 2m 41s'. Right canvas assembles live section-by-section rather than sitting empty. Close with a summary that names what was decided, in design vocabulary, so the user's next instruction is 'warmer than that' rather than 'I don't like it'.
adopt.rationale: GoDaddy's sibling builder shows 'Worked for 45s' with a filling checklist including 'Applied gelato color theme — Paired with bubblegum fonts', and a reviewer explicitly noted the difference from builders that show nothing. v0 badges 'Worked for 6m 21s' as evidence of effort. Naming the palette and font pairing gives a non-designer the vocabulary to steer the next prompt — which is the whole game after the first render. And a 2m41s badge is a competitive statement when v0 prints 6m21s.

adopt.pattern: Publish a zero-credit action list — and stop billing credits for publishing
adopt.spec: Tooltip on the persistent credits chip in the top toolbar, and a matching line in the KB, reading: 'Free, always: previewing, publishing and republishing, editing text and swapping images directly on the page, restoring an earlier version, and any fix for a mistake Remixer made.' Make direct-manipulation edits genuinely free by writing them to source without an agent call, escalating to metered chat only when scope exceeds text/image/colour/spacing. Add an 'It's on us' badge on any auto-repair turn.
adopt.rationale: This is our sharpest competitive exposure. Lovable publishes free on every plan and states 'Publishing itself is free'; Bolt's security audits and version restores cost no tokens; GoDaddy documents an explicit no-credit list covering Preview, Code, Edit, media upload and History restore; Base44 exempts all manual visual edits and database reads/writes; Figma Make stages direct manipulation credit-free until you press apply; Lovable gives 100 free inline text edits per user per day. Remixer currently bills credits for generation, chat edits AND publishing — taxing the moment of success is the harshest placement in the field, and the low-grade 'is this click costing me money' anxiety is what suppresses the exploration that produces a site the user is proud of.

adopt.pattern: A daily credit drip so the trial has a rhythm and a reason to return tomorrow
adopt.spec: Grant every trial and paid account a small daily allowance on top of the monthly pool. Surface it as a second chip beside the credits chip: '+25 today · resets 3am PT', with the tooltip 'Free daily credits. They don't roll over — use them or lose them.' On return after 24h idle, the builder opens on a short re-entry card above the chat: 'Welcome back. Your daily credits are topped up. Want to pick up where you left off?' with two buttons — 'Continue <project name>' and 'Start something new'. Spend order must be documented and drain daily grants first.
adopt.rationale: Every leader runs this loop and Remixer runs none: Lovable grants 5 daily build credits resetting 00:00 UTC on Free, Pro and Business; v0 Plus gives '$2 of free daily credits on login per user' — a literal login reward; Framer resets 500 credits daily; Bolt resets 300K tokens daily; Replit gives free daily Agent credits; Base44 resets 5/day at midnight in the owner's timezone. A pure monthly allowance gives a user who stalls on day 2 no reason to open the tab on day 3, and our 30-day window then expires quietly.

adopt.pattern: End the first session with a real, shareable address — and say the trial rule out loud
adopt.spec: The moment the first build completes, dock a persistent bar under the preview: the *.remixer.app URL with a copy button, 'Open in a new tab', 'Text it to myself', and the line 'Live now on your free Remixer address. Free for 30 days — no card. Connect your own domain any time.' Make the subdomain rename pencil visible in this bar, not only in the toolbar, and pre-fill it from the business name the AI just generated. Any credit-cost language must be absent from this bar.
adopt.rationale: GoDaddy's free tier can build but cannot publish at all, and reviewers judge its long autogenerated subdomain 'not viable for a professional business presence' — meaning their free user's first session ends with nothing they can show anyone. Replit made free-tier publishing a headline ('publish up to 1 project') and Google AI Studio ships free name.ai.studio subdomains. Our trial permits preview publishing, which is a genuine advantage we currently state only in a four-step explainer rather than at the moment it lands. Hostinger's publish flow even plays a completion sound and immediately offers 'Copy URL' and 'Go to Analytics' — the finish line should be a beginning.

avoid.pattern: Gating all output behind signup, and putting a survey inside the gap
avoid.why: Bolt's own quickstart sequences it: paste prompt → 'Build now' → 'Sign in or sign up (Google, GitHub, or email: no credit card required)' → complete a survey → wait 'approximately five minutes while Bolt creates your app.' Nothing renders anonymously, so the user commits four to six actions and five minutes before seeing a single pixel. GoDaddy runs both patterns simultaneously — legacy Websites+Marketing walls first, the newer Airo AI Builder walls after the prompt — which tells you which way the company decided the arrow points.

avoid.pattern: A decorative hero composer that isn't a real input
avoid.why: Base44's homepage renders an animated fake composer cycling 'Build'/'Send' against rotating nouns [Apps][Websites][Games][Tools], and every CTA ('Start building', 'Build an app', 'Create an AI agent') hands off to app.base44.com. It wastes the single highest-intent moment in the funnel and forfeits Lovable's advantage of the marketing page BEING the product's primary control. If Remixer's marketing composer ever stops carrying its prompt into the builder, it degrades into exactly this.

avoid.pattern: Holding the user hostage during generation
avoid.why: A Wix Harmony reviewer documented a mid-generation modal reading 'Don't leave this tab', warning that switching tabs would interrupt the build — converting a 4–7 minute wait into 4–7 minutes of enforced attention. The correct model is Lovable's manipulable message queue and mobile push ('get notified when a build is ready to review'), which turn the wait into productive time instead of a hostage situation.

avoid.pattern: An empty preview pane for the entire build
avoid.why: In a first-hand v0 run the right canvas showed only the v0 logomark and 'Your v0 generation will show here.' for all 6m 21s, with every signal confined to the chat column. Even GoDaddy's weaker sibling builder beats this with a narrated 'Matching styles to your industry…' status and a filling checklist, and its reviewer's verdict is the lesson: 'you are not staring at a blank progress bar either.'

avoid.pattern: A free tier that cannot produce anything shareable
avoid.why: GoDaddy Airo AI Builder's Free plan gives unlimited building and 50 credits but 'can only build, not publish'; reviewers report the 50 credits exhausted in roughly six prompts at ~8 credits/prompt, with one hitting the ceiling 'as soon as our website was finished'. The user reaches the emotional peak — a finished site — and is blocked from the one action that makes it real.

avoid.pattern: Daily micro-caps that end the first session before the first session ends
avoid.why: Base44's Free plan is 5 message credits per DAY (25/month), which a Product Hunt reviewer said 'you'll burn through just tweaking UI'. Bolt's free 300K tokens/day is reported by reviewers to run out 'before a first build finishes' against Bolt's own five-minute build estimate. Figma caps Starter and View seats at 500/month plus 150/day. A cap that fires mid-first-build converts curiosity directly into abandonment.

avoid.pattern: Asking for the domain before the user has seen anything
avoid.why: Hostinger Horizons' own tutorial sequences hPanel → 'Add website' → Horizons → prompt → 'choose a domain or use a temporary one' — the domain decision is pulled in front of the build. GoDaddy's other funnel monetises at step 2, before the site exists. A domain is a name commitment; asking for it before the user has a site to attach it to raises the emotional cost of a step that should be trivially cheap, and it is the one step Remixer can make near-frictionless later.

avoid.pattern: Leaking raw errors and dev-server internals to non-technical users
avoid.why: Base44's own troubleshooting doc lists what users actually see: 'Failed to load app: Error serializing to JSON: UnicodeEncodeError' (triggered by characters in an app NAME) and "'dict' object has no attribute 'lower'" — a Python AttributeError shown to someone sold no-code. A GoDaddy reviewer pasting a long PRD hit a raw 'Bad Request', and GoDaddy's official prompt guide lists the fix for a broken preview as prompting 'Restart dev server'. Bolt goes further and tells users to open the browser console ('On macOS: press CMD + Option + J').

avoid.pattern: Hiding the credit balance away from the work surface
avoid.why: GoDaddy requires User menu → 'Manage my plan' → 'Total AI Credit Usage' to see a balance; a hands-on reviewer called it 'a nuisance' and named it a top complaint, noting that other builders show a running tally on the dashboard. Remixer's persistent credits chip in the top toolbar is already the correct answer — the anti-pattern to avoid is ever moving it, or shipping a credit cost the user cannot see before they act.

avoid.pattern: Charging the user for your own mistakes, and for the moment of success
avoid.why: Lovable makes 'Try to fix', 'Try to fix all', both security scan depths and design-system verification turns free 'within our fair use policy', plus 100 free inline text edits per user per day; GoDaddy's agent repairs its own validation errors without consuming credits; Bolt's security audits and version restores cost zero tokens. Meanwhile unpredictable burn is the single most-cited complaint on every one of these platforms — G2 on Lovable ('Credits can disappear pretty quickly'), Trustpilot on Bolt at a reported 1.4/5, Vercel Community's 'Credits are burning way too fast'. Remixer billing credits on publish sits on the wrong side of every one of these precedents.

leapfrog.idea: Claim the name while it builds — turn the 2–3 minute wait into the domain purchase moment
leapfrog.spec: The generation agent names the business before it writes components (v0 invented 'Ember & Oak' unprompted; GoDaddy's Airo domain flow starts from business-name suggestions). The instant that name exists — roughly 15 seconds in — fire a live DreamHost availability check and dock a card in the lower-right of the canvas while the build continues: headline 'emberandoak.com is available', three alternates beneath it with prices, and two buttons: 'Claim it — $X for the first year' and 'Not now'. Purchasing never leaves the builder and never interrupts the build; on completion the site publishes to the new domain with zero DNS steps because we are the registrar and the host, and the toolbar's centred domain switcher flips from remixer.app to the real name with a green 'Live' dot. If the user declines, show the card once more at first publish and never again.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: It requires sub-second registrar availability data, in-house checkout, and a builder that stalls the user for two to three minutes — a combination only a registrar-host has. GoDaddy owns the registrar and still makes users leave: its documented buy flow is 'Go to GoDaddy domains, search for a desired domain, and then purchase it', then return to the Airo apps page, select the app, Domain, Settings, Connect Domain. Bolt, Emergent and Replit resell someone else's registry (Name.com, IONOS, an upstream) and can only offer purchase as a post-build settings step. Nobody has thought of the wait as inventory.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost is the registrar, the host and the DNS operator. We can price it, sell it, and attach it with literally zero DNS steps — and we are the only builder in the field whose generation wait is short enough to be pleasant but long enough to fill.

leapfrog.idea: Ship a working mailbox as part of the wow, not as an upsell after it
leapfrog.spec: At first publish, a single button beneath the live URL: 'Create hello@emberandoak.com'. One click provisions a real DreamHost mailbox, rewires the site's contact form to deliver to it, and sends a test message the user watches land in an inline inbox preview inside the builder — three lines of it, with the subject 'Your first message'. Copy underneath: 'Real inbox, real address. Included in your plan.' If the domain isn't DreamHost-held yet, the button becomes the domain-claim card from leapfrog 1. Include the mailbox in the $9.99 Build plan rather than laddering it, and say so on the pricing card as a bullet: 'A real @yourdomain mailbox — included.'
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: None of them operate mail. Bolt's entire domains documentation set contains no mention of mailboxes — it will sell you a domain at checkout and leave you to buy Google Workspace. Base44's docs state flatly 'Custom email domains are for sending only'. Lovable sends 50,000 DKIM/SPF/DMARC-authenticated emails a month from your domain and its docs are explicit that it 'does not provide mailboxes'. v0 has no email product at any tier. GoDaddy resells Microsoft 365 at $7.99/mo or its own at $2.99/user/mo — its comparison table concedes 'Professional email: Yes — Purchase required'. Hostinger is the only one bundling mailboxes and it ladders them 1/2/5 by tier as a paywall lever.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost runs its own mail platform, so a mailbox costs us marginal cents and costs competitors a reseller margin they must recover with an upsell. It converts time-to-wow from 'I have a website' to 'I have a business address' — a materially bigger emotional payoff for the trades and small-business segment the starter chips target.

leapfrog.idea: 'Already yours' onboarding — the first screen is their inventory, not a blank prompt
leapfrog.spec: For any visitor with a DreamHost session, replace the blank composer above the fold with a short card stack of what they already own: 'You own bakerystreet.com — and we host it. Want Remixer to rebuild it?' with a thumbnail of the current site and three buttons: 'Rebuild it', 'Build something new for it', 'Start from scratch'. 'Rebuild it' pre-populates the composer with a brief generated from the existing site's own headings, services and copy, attaches the domain before generation, and publishes with zero DNS steps. Include a one-line consent notice: 'We'll read the public pages of your site to write the brief. Nothing changes until you publish.' For domains registered but not hosted, the card reads 'You own thisname.com and nothing is on it yet.' — the highest-intent user in the entire funnel.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: It requires an existing customer inventory of owned domains AND hosted content, joined to the builder. GoDaddy holds the same position and ships only a generic 'Rebuild my site' chip that requires the user to paste a URL; its own docs still route domain purchase out to the storefront. Lovable, Bolt, v0 and Base44 have no idea what their users already own. Wix and Hostinger have inventories but bury the builder behind their control panels rather than leading with the inventory.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost has hundreds of thousands of parked domains and ageing hosted sites — a warm base for whom the blank-prompt problem does not exist and for whom 'connect a domain' is already solved. It is the only onboarding path in the category that starts at step three.

leapfrog.idea: Guarantee zero DNS steps — and buy the fallback so we're never the last builder handing out a record table
leapfrog.spec: Two moves. (a) For DreamHost-held domains, allow publishing to a live custom domain during the free trial, badged in the publish sheet: '0 DNS steps. It's your domain and our nameservers.' with a status ladder of Provisioning → Issuing SSL → Live, and a recovery verb on every failure state. (b) For external domains, license Entri — the same service Replit uses — so we sign into the user's registrar and write records for them; and separately implement Domain Connect as a PROVIDER so third-party apps can attach to DreamHost-held domains in one click, turning our registrar base into an acquisition surface. Until (b) ships, every failure state in the guided-DNS flow needs a button, on Lovable's model: Verifying → 'Check status', Stalled → 'Retry', Offline → 'Recover', Removed → 'Reconnect', plus the Cloudflare-specific line 'Set the record to DNS only (grey cloud), not Proxied.'
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Everyone stops at the boundary of what they own. Bolt is entirely manual even for domains bought through Bolt — www CNAME plus root ALIAS/ANAME to site-dns.bolt.host, 'up to 24 hours', manual 'Verify domain status'. Base44's external flow exposes that it runs on Render (base44.onrender.com, 216.24.57.1), demands users delete AAAA and CAA records, and sends them to whatsmydns.net. GoDaddy invented Domain Connect and open-sourced it to ~50 companies, yet its own external flow is still manual. Replit — not a registrar at all — solved it by buying Entri.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: Our verified Aug 2026 Domain Connect gap is currently a liability that a non-registrar (Replit) has already closed off the shelf. Fixing it is table stakes; becoming a Domain Connect PROVIDER is the leapfrog, because it makes every DreamHost domain the easiest domain in the world to attach to anything — which is a reason to register with us rather than with GoDaddy.

leapfrog.idea: Put the first prompt inside other people's AI assistants via MCP
leapfrog.spec: Ship a DreamHost MCP server exposing three tools: check domain availability with pricing, reserve a name for 30 minutes, and start a Remixer build from a natural-language brief. In Claude or ChatGPT a user says 'I need a site for my dog-grooming business' and gets availability, a claim link, and a build link that lands them in the Remixer builder with the site already generating and their assistant conversation's brief pre-loaded as the first chat message. Sign the handoff so account creation happens once, on arrival, with the prompt already carried.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: GoDaddy shipped domain search into Claude via MCP on 14 Feb 2026 with the framing 'Naming your business shouldn't feel like an interruption', and has published a roadmap of authenticated domain management and expansion to OpenAI, Google and Perplexity — but it stops at search, because its builder cannot accept a prompt handoff and its domain purchase requires the storefront. Nobody has connected assistant-side intent to a running generation.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: We control the registrar (availability + checkout), the builder (accepts a brief), and the host (publishes with no DNS), so we can complete the entire idea→available name→built site→live URL loop from inside a third-party assistant. It moves top-of-funnel to where naming conversations actually happen now, and it is exactly the distribution move GoDaddy has started and cannot finish.

open_questions: Does a prompt typed on dreamhost.com/remixer today survive DreamHost SSO and start generating on arrival, or does the user land in the panel and retype? Measure the drop between composer_submit and generation_start — this is the single largest unquantified leak in the lens.

What is our real production time-to-first-render at p50 and p90, not the marketing 2–3 minutes? If p90 is 5 minutes we are level with Bolt and the speed claim stops being a weapon; if p50 is genuinely 2m40s we should print the elapsed badge on every build.

Do credits currently get consumed when a trial user publishes to *.remixer.app, or only on custom-domain publish? If staging publish is free we must say so at the moment of publish; if it is metered, that is the first thing to change.

What happens to a built-but-unpublished site on day 31 of the trial? GoDaddy takes downgraded sites offline while explicitly preserving content and restoring it on re-engagement or upgrade. Do we delete, freeze, or preserve — and does the user know before day 31?

Should the free tier become perpetual with a small daily grant rather than a 30-day window? Every direct competitor now runs perpetual free (Lovable, v0, Bolt, Base44, GoDaddy, Framer, Replit); our 30-day no-card window is the longest trial in a category that has stopped running trials.

What is the marginal credit and latency cost of generating three design directions before the build, and can it fit inside the 2–3 minute promise — or do we ship the cheaper post-build 'Try other looks' variant that Google AI Studio proves works in one click?

What share of trial signups already hold a DreamHost domain, and what share already host a site with us? That number sizes the 'Already yours' leapfrog and determines whether it is the default first screen or a secondary path.
Do our terms and privacy posture permit reading a customer's own hosted public pages to pre-write a rebuild brief, and what consent string does legal require in-flow?

What does Domain Connect support cost us to build, and is licensing Entri (Replit's route) faster to ship than implementing the spec ourselves — given we would also want to be a Domain Connect provider for inbound acquisition?

Can a real @yourdomain mailbox be included in the $9.99 Build plan without cannibalising DreamHost's existing email revenue, or does it need to be one included mailbox with paid additions (Hostinger's 1/2/5 ladder)?

Who owns the first-session re-engagement email sequence, and do we currently send anything at all between abandoned signup, first build, and day 30? Lovable and Base44 both push notifications on build completion; we have no documented equivalent.

What does our first render actually look like against the field on the same prompt? Run a blind side-by-side of Remixer, Lovable, v0 and Base44 on five real small-business briefs and score them for 'would you show this to a customer' before investing in the design-directions step.

executive_take:
The category has converged on one skeleton — chat left, canvas right, Publish top-right — so competition has moved to three harder questions: how you get from the canvas to the dozen other surfaces a real site needs; how the shell survives growth from one page to forty files; and where the free/paid line is drawn inside the chrome.

On navigation, four incompatible answers exist. Lovable uses a horizontal Preview/Files/Code/More toolbar with eight destinations nested under "More". Bolt hides an entire IDE plus a terminal behind one top-centre `<>` icon, framed as "shaped to feel approachable for anyone who wants to dig deeper." Base44 makes the backend a separate Dashboard *mode* — ten-plus sections, a genuine second application. v0 uses a five-icon top-bar cluster and hands off to the Vercel dashboard for anything real. The strongest external signal is Replit's 31 July 2026 note: "The new pinned Tools pane brings Database, Auth, Domains, Secrets, and more together in a single place." That is convergence onto Remixer's right icon rail. Nobody has done it elegantly yet; this is winnable ground.

On scaling, the field is weak and Base44 is alone in taking it seriously: a type-to-search page dropdown that holds 600 pages, and "Files used in this page" — a reverse lookup that lets a non-coder find the right file without reading a tree. Base44 and Replit independently converged on an infinite canvas of live page frames. Lovable answers with Expand all/Collapse all, Search code, ⌘⇧F and ⌘⇧L line references: IDE hygiene, not novice IA.

On keyboard, only Lovable is IDE-grade — ⌘K palette searching projects *and settings*, ⌘B collapsing chat panel and dashboard sidebar with the same key, Opt+P plan/build, single-key S/T/D/C. Bolt ships one shortcut (Ctrl+S). GoDaddy ships none while advertising to "Developers".

Remixer already leads in two places: a persistent credits chip (GoDaddy exiles it to a separate page, Base44 hides it behind the logo, Bolt behind Profile→Subscription) and — uniquely in the field — a domain switcher in permanent top-bar chrome. Everyone else buries domains in settings because attaching one takes hours and may fail. Ours can resolve in seconds because we are the registrar. That chip is our most defensible IA asset and it is badly under-exploited. We are behind on: no command palette, no documented panel resize, no agent blast-radius controls, no multi-page overview, and credits burning on publish — the one place every rival has drawn the free line on the other side.

comparison.approach: Chat left / preview right, no rail. Navigation is a horizontal four-tab project toolbar (Preview / Files / Code / More) with eight destinations nested under More: Analytics, Cloud, Agent integrations, Payments, Connectors, Security, SEO & AI search, Sensitive data. Top bar left-to-right: logo (opens dashboard sidebar) → project-name menu carrying workspace/plan/credits → History toggle → Close sidebar. Right: preview-toolbar button, comments, collaborator avatars, Share, Publish (collapses to an icon on narrow windows). IDE-grade keyboard: ⌘K command palette searching projects AND settings, ⌘B collapses chat panel (and the dashboard sidebar — same key, same meaning), Opt+P Build↔Plan, Opt+V dictate, ⌘⇧F project search, ⌘⇧L exact line reference, single-key S/T/D/C for the draggable preview toolbar. Mobile app swipes between chat and preview.
comparison.notes: Only product with a real command palette and a consistent collapse shortcut across two different shells. Deploy state expressed three coherent ways (dot on Publish, 'Published' badge in History, stated snapshot model). Gaps: panel width/resize is undocumented and unverifiable behind auth (I checked docs directly — no resize affordance described); no file-locking or agent scoping; no multi-page overview.

comparison.approach: The only competitor whose layout maths are declared in CSS: --chat-default-width 450px, --chat-min-width = default, --header-height 50px, --panel-header-height 50px (deliberately matched so the seam reads as one band), --side-menu-width 35px, --workbench-width calc(100% - chat), --workbench-inner-width minus 1rem so the preview floats. Chat is drag-resizable with a handle tinted rgb(brand / 50%); in chat-only pre-generation mode it expands to clamp(720px, 50vw, 1024px). Top bar splits three ways with an unusual CENTRE cluster: database, gear ('All project settings'), `<>` Code Preview, device preview, and a version-history clock — which was explicitly MOVED from the project title menu into the top nav in the 13–19 July 2026 release. Right: Share, Publish, GitHub. The entire IDE — file tree, CodeMirror editor, and a bottom drawer with Bolt / Publish Output / Terminal tabs — hides behind that single `<>`.
comparison.notes: Best progressive disclosure in the field and the only one with user-controllable agent blast radius (right-click → Target file / Lock file / Lock all under 'Guide Bolt's focus'). Fails on keyboard: Ctrl+S is the only documented shortcut, no command palette. Shell degrades silently by environment — 'Code view, project settings, and database access are unavailable on mobile devices', and Safari code view is read-only.

comparison.approach: Three zones: chat left, preview right, and a Dashboard reached as a separate MODE (Overview, Data, Security, Domains, Analytics, SEO & GEO, Logs, Workflows, Code with Functions and Secrets, Settings). Top bar carries preview, dashboard, code, testing, a Theme palette icon, a Canvas icon, device switcher, a type-to-search page dropdown, and Publish top-right. Canvas is the standout: an infinite board where every page renders as a live-preview frame at desktop/tablet/phone with Figma-grade shortcuts (V/H/D/N/I, ⌘1 fit, ⌘0 100%, ⇧⌘L lock), hover-revealed edge handles for arrow connections, per-frame viewport dropdowns, and real-time multiplayer. ⌘. cycles Default/Discuss/Edit chat modes 'even while you're typing a prompt.' Code tab offers 'Files used in this page' grouped by project location plus 'See all files'.
comparison.notes: Alone in taking scale seriously — 600-page ceiling with a searchable switcher, plus the best novice bridge in the field (reverse file lookup). Penalised because Dashboard-as-a-mode is a full context switch out of the build loop, credit balance is hidden behind clicking the logo, and branch mode strips most of the shell (publishing, secrets, connectors, workflows, code editor, theme settings and version-history restore all disabled).

comparison.approach: Two panes with an unusually narrow chat rail — roughly 25% of viewport (~320px CSS at 1280). Top bar: v0 mark → favourite star → auto-generated chat title with chevron → collapse-chat chevron → a five-icon cluster (comments, eye/preview, design mode, code, database) → then a real browser chrome strip: back, forward, device toggle, editable URL field showing the route, open-in-new, refresh. Code view is a full VS Code clone: three-tab left rail (explorer/search/git), file tree headed V0-PROJECT with new-file/new-folder/refresh/collapse-all, and an empty-editor state that teaches four shortcuts with rendered keycaps — Go to File ⌘P, Find in Files ⇧⌘F, Command Palette ⇧⌘P, Terminal ^`.
comparison.notes: Real browser chrome (not a device-frame mock) is the best preview affordance in the field, and the shortcut-teaching empty state is the cheapest onboarding win anywhere. But every icon in that top cluster ships with aria-label AND title null — icon-only chrome with no accessible names. Anything operational (domains, analytics, env vars) leaves the shell for the Vercel dashboard, and the preview pane stays empty for the full 6m21s build.

comparison.approach: Split-panel Agent pane / preview, but with the most deliberate IA consolidation in the field: the 31 July 2026 release note reads 'The new pinned Tools pane brings Database, Auth, Domains, Secrets, and more together in a single place.' The right pane is artifact-aware — for agents and automations it becomes an admin dashboard instead of a preview. Agent 4 replaced the Design Mode tab with an infinite Design Canvas 'that sits at the center of the design workflow', moved collaboration from fork-and-merge to one shared project with per-person threads and a shared Kanban (Drafts / Active / Ready / Done), and allows opening a planning chat while the main build still runs.
comparison.notes: Direct external validation of Remixer's right-rail bet, plus two ideas nobody else has: swapping the right pane's meaning by artifact type, and a parallel planning thread during a live build. Docs are thin on pane mechanics (I fetched the workspace doc — no resize, docking or palette detail). Workspace complexity is high for a novice audience.

comparison.approach: The mirror image of everyone else: AI chat on the RIGHT, site-management sidebar on the LEFT behind a hamburger (Monthly AI credits with a usage graph, upgrade/top-up links, Create new website, Duplicate this website, Account sharing), live preview centre. Top nav is just 'Ask AI' and 'Publish'. The centre canvas has a four-way toggle — Preview / Edit content / Code / Data — exposing the DATABASE as a peer tab rather than a buried tool. Best panel behaviour measured anywhere: drag the chat edge to resize and 'your preferred width is saved'; drag the handle fully to one side to hide the panel; double-click the handle to reset to default.
comparison.notes: One drag handle doing three jobs with persistence is the single most directly copyable shell detail in this sweep. Undermined by mode-gating the shell on price — the code editor and file tree appear only at Hobbyist $39.99/mo, so Explorer and Starter users cannot see part of their own shell and must spend a credit on every CSS tweak. Undo and Restore are destructive and permanently delete messages.

comparison.approach: Chat left, canvas centre, and a RIGHT properties panel added 30 July 2026 carrying a full DOM tree ('layers view for code') with spacing, padding, typography, layout, opacity, z-index, borders, corner radius and colour/type tokens bound to the codebase — plus multi-select of every instance of an element. Top-right toolbar toggles 'Edit' and 'Annotate for agent' (numbered blue on-canvas callouts). Device frames switch while editing, not only in a separate preview mode. Critically, direct manipulations stage in the prompt box credit-free until applied.
comparison.notes: The only product where a design-tool-grade right inspector coexists with a chat panel, which is the layout Remixer's rail could grow into. Scored down because there is NO file-level version history — versions are builds inside the chat, recovered by scrolling and clicking 'Restore this version', with a standing forum feature request for real history.

comparison.approach: Left chat with History docked directly beneath the chat window; centre canvas; an uppermost six-item mode bar — Preview / Edit / Code / Menu / Media / Settings. Settings contains only two things: Database and Secrets. Device switching is a current-state-labelled dropdown top-right, plus a manual 'Refresh Preview' button and 'View & Share'. Publish is a bare upper-right button with no modal. Element selection raises a floating white segmented toolbar: Replace | Modify | On click | bookmark | AI sparkle.
comparison.notes: Two genuinely good ideas — a two-item Settings that bets everything else is reachable by prompt, and 'On click' as an inline behaviour control. Everything else is legacy drag: Menu and Media are two separate asset surfaces in a six-item bar; the same control is named 'Preview Desktop' in one doc and 'Change device' in another; zero keyboard shortcuts anywhere despite an audience rail addressed to 'Developers'; the credit balance is exiled to a separate 'Manage my plan' page (a reviewer called it 'a nuisance'); and the documented fix for a broken preview is to prompt 'Restart dev server'.

comparison.approach: Dark #18181B shell held consistently from entry through build (GoDaddy, by contrast, switches from a dark violet entry screen to a light builder). Top toolbar: logo, 'Visual Editor', a CENTERED DOMAIN SWITCHER, credits chip, blue #1587FF Publish, avatar. Left AI chat panel at ~408px, right icon rail, centre canvas/preview. 2–3 minute first generation — the fastest in the field, against Bolt's documented ~5 min, Base44's 3–5, Wix Harmony's 4–7 and v0's measured 6m21s.
comparison.notes: Two things we already lead on: a persistent credits chip in the toolbar (everyone else hides it), and the only domain control in permanent top-bar chrome in the entire field. The right rail is structurally correct — Replit converged on it in July 2026. Against that: no command palette, no documented panel resize or collapse, no agent blast-radius controls, no multi-page overview, and publishing burns credits, which is the single worst free/paid boundary in the category.

best_in_class.why: On this lens specifically, Lovable wins on control and coherence rather than on features. Three concrete reasons. (1) It is the only product with a genuine command palette that indexes more than files: ⌘K searches projects AND settings, so the shell has a single universal entrance and the tab bar never has to grow. (2) Its shortcuts are semantically consistent across two different shells — ⌘B collapses the chat panel in the editor and the sidebar in the dashboard, so the key means 'give me more canvas' everywhere, and Opt+P (Build↔Plan) plus single-key S/T/D/C for preview modes give it an IDE-grade vocabulary that Bolt (one shortcut) and GoDaddy (none) cannot touch. (3) It expresses one system state — 'live is stale' — in three places without contradiction: a dot on the Publish button, a 'Published' badge on the live version in History, and the plainly-stated snapshot model in docs. That coherence is what stops a shell feeling like a bundle of features. Its IA restraint helps too: eight secondary destinations sit nested under a single 'More' tab rather than fragmenting the toolbar, and toolbar navigation was explicitly polished for keyboard on 26 May 2026. The honest caveat is that Lovable is beaten on scaling: Base44 is the one to beat there, with a type-to-search 600-page switcher, a 'Files used in this page' reverse lookup, and an infinite Canvas of live page frames. If we only copy one shell, copy Lovable's control layer; if we want to win at forty files, copy Base44's.

adopt.pattern: ⌘K command palette as the shell's universal entrance
adopt.spec: ⌘K / Ctrl+K opens a 560px-wide centred overlay on a blurred #18181B/70 scrim, 12px radius, 1px zinc-800 border. Input at 15px with placeholder 'Search pages, files, settings, or type a command'. Results grouped with 11px/600 uppercase zinc-500 headers at 0.06em tracking, in fixed order: Pages (route in JetBrains Mono 12px zinc-500 on the right of each row), Files, Actions, Settings, Recent. Actions ship verbatim as: 'Publish changes', 'Connect a domain', 'Create a mailbox', 'Open database', 'View version history', 'Toggle live preview', 'Buy credits'. Selected row gets a #1587FF 2px left bar and zinc-800 fill; ↵ executes, ⌘↵ opens in a new tab, Esc closes. Also reachable by a magnifier glyph at the far left of the top toolbar so it is discoverable without knowing the key. Every command must also be a real UI control somewhere — the palette is an accelerator, never the only path.
adopt.rationale: Lovable is the only competitor with one (⌘K searching projects AND settings) and it is why its toolbar can stay at four tabs while carrying eight nested destinations. A palette is the only IA mechanism that lets the shell absorb new surfaces without growing the rail. Remixer has none.

adopt.pattern: Right rail with a labelled expanded state and a lifecycle-ordered grouping
adopt.spec: Rail is 56px collapsed / 240px expanded, toggled by a persistent chevron at the rail's top and by ⌥\ ; state persists per user. Every icon carries an aria-label and a tooltip on a 200ms hover delay. Order the rail by the user's lifecycle, not by feature age, with 1px zinc-800 dividers and (in the expanded state only) 11px/600 uppercase zinc-500 group labels at 0.06em tracking: BUILD — Pages, Media; DATA — Database, Forms, Accounts, File uploads; MONEY — Payments, Shipping; SHIP — Domains, Email, Analytics, Activity logs; KEYS — API keys, Settings. Group labels are the copy; do not invent cute names. A rail item that is empty shows a 6px zinc-600 dot rather than nothing, so absence reads as 'not set up yet' rather than 'broken'.
adopt.rationale: Replit's 31 July 2026 release note — 'The new pinned Tools pane brings Database, Auth, Domains, Secrets, and more together in a single place' — is direct validation that a pinned tools surface beats scattered menus. The failure mode is a junk drawer of unlabelled glyphs, which is exactly what v0 shipped: aria-label and title both null across its entire builder toolbar cluster.

adopt.pattern: Resizable, collapsible chat panel with persisted width and one shortcut that means one thing
adopt.spec: Chat panel default 408px, min 360px, max 720px. A 4px-wide invisible drag hit-target on its right edge; on hover it reveals a 2px vertical bar at #1587FF/50 (copy Bolt's --chat-resize-handle-background-color idea exactly). Width persists per user. Double-clicking the handle resets to 408px. Dragging fully left collapses the panel to a 48px stub showing only the Remixer AI gradient glyph and a right-chevron. ⌘B toggles collapse — and must use the same key on the project dashboard to collapse the project sidebar, so the shortcut means 'give me more canvas' everywhere.
adopt.rationale: Bolt declares --chat-default-width: 450px with a brand-tinted drag handle; Hostinger Horizons persists the width, hides on full drag, and resets on double-click — one handle doing three jobs. Lovable collapses with ⌘B but its docs describe no resize at all (verified directly). Remixer's ~408px is fixed, which is wrong for both chat-heavy and canvas-heavy sessions.

adopt.pattern: Single-control code disclosure in the top bar, with one reassurance line
adopt.spec: Promote a `</>` glyph to the top toolbar, immediately right of the domain switcher, that swaps the canvas for code; an eye glyph returns. Do not put code in the rail as one icon among fifteen — it needs to read as a mode, not a tool. The first time a user opens it, show a single dismissible 32px strip above the file tree, zinc-900 fill, 13px text: 'This is your site's real code. Nothing you do here reaches visitors until you publish.' with an × on the right. File tree needs Expand all / Collapse all and a 'Search files' box from day one.
adopt.rationale: Bolt's entire IDE — file tree, editor, and a bottom drawer with agent log / publish output / terminal — hides behind one top-centre `<>`, framed in its own docs as 'shaped to feel approachable for anyone who wants to dig deeper.' It is the cleanest solution in the category to showing code without scaring novices. Lovable added Expand all / Collapse all on 13 July 2026 because trees get unusable fast.

adopt.pattern: Searchable page switcher in canvas chrome, plus a 'Files on this page' reverse lookup
adopt.spec: A pill in the canvas chrome (NOT the top bar — the top bar belongs to the domain) showing the current route: `/pricing ▾` in JetBrains Mono 13px. Clicking opens a 320px list with a filter field at the top, placeholder 'Filter pages'; each row shows the page title at 14px and the route beneath in mono 12px zinc-500. A pinned footer row reads 'Files on this page (4)' — clicking it opens the code panel pre-filtered to exactly those files, grouped by folder, with a 'See all files' link back out. Search must match on both title and route.
adopt.rationale: Base44 is the only competitor that has designed for scale: its page dropdown supports typing to search and holds up to 600 pages, and its Code tab offers 'Files used in this page' grouped by project location with 'See all files'. That reverse lookup is the single best bridge in the field between a non-coder's mental model (a page) and the file system. Nothing in Remixer today carries a user from one page to forty files.

adopt.pattern: Agent blast-radius controls: Focus and Lock, on right-click in both the page switcher and the file tree
adopt.spec: Right-click any page or file. Menu section header reads 'Guide Remixer's focus'. Two items: 'Focus on this page' — pins agent attention and renders a chip above the chat composer, #1587FF/16 fill with a #1587FF pin glyph, reading 'Focused: /pricing' with an × to clear. And 'Lock' — sets an amber padlock glyph on the row; the agent then refuses and says so in chat verbatim: 'app/pricing/page.tsx is locked. Unlock it, or tell me where else to make this change.' A directory-level 'Lock all' matches Bolt. Locked/focused state persists across sessions and shows in the file tree at a glance.
adopt.rationale: Bolt ships exactly this (right-click → 'Target file' / 'Lock file' / 'Lock all', with the rationale 'You'll get more accurate results if you're explicit about what Bolt should and shouldn't change'); Base44 ships 'Freeze Files'. One context menu answers three separate complaints at once — the AI touched something I didn't ask about, it broke another page, and it burned my credits re-reading everything. Lovable does not have it. Remixer does not have it.

adopt.pattern: Version history promoted into the top bar, immediately left of Publish
adopt.spec: A clock glyph sitting immediately left of the blue Publish button. When the canvas differs from live, a 6px amber dot sits on the clock's upper right. Hover tooltip: 'Last published 14 min ago · 3 changes since'. Clicking opens a right-side panel, not a modal, so the canvas stays visible; each entry shows the prompt that produced it, a relative timestamp, and per-row 'Preview' and 'Restore' buttons. The currently live entry carries a green 'Live' badge. Restoring must NOT auto-publish — the confirmation copy reads 'Restored. This is a draft — select Publish to make it live.'
adopt.rationale: Bolt explicitly moved version history out of the project title menu and INTO the top navigation in the 13–19 July 2026 release — a deliberate promotion. Lovable puts a History toggle in the top bar's left cluster and badges the live version 'Published'. GoDaddy decouples restore from publish with the same instruction ('Once restored, select Publish to make it live'), which is the correct model: rollback is done in panic and must be previewable.

adopt.pattern: One deploy state, said three ways in three places
adopt.spec: (a) A 6px amber dot on the Publish button whenever the canvas differs from live. (b) A state pill immediately right of the centred domain switcher: green dot + 'Live' when in sync, amber dot + 'Draft changes' when not, indigo + 'Not connected' when only on *.remixer.app. Clicking the pill opens the history panel scrolled to the live version. (c) One sentence inside the Publish menu, above the button: 'Publishing takes a snapshot. Changes you make after this don't reach visitors until you publish again.' All three must derive from the same state value — never let them disagree.
adopt.rationale: Lovable expresses this exact fact three coherent ways (dot on Publish, 'Published' badge in History, stated snapshot model) and staging-vs-live confusion is the most common support cost in site builders. Remixer already owns the colour semantics for it — green = live, amber = action needed — and is currently spending them on nothing at this level.

adopt.pattern: A 'Live preview' toggle in the canvas overflow
adopt.spec: In the canvas chrome overflow menu, a switch labelled 'Live preview', default on, with helper text beneath at 12px zinc-500: 'When off, the canvas shows your last completed build.' When off, the canvas gets a 24px amber-tinted strip at the top reading 'Showing last completed build' with a 'Show live' link. State persists per project.
adopt.rationale: Lovable shipped precisely this on 6 August 2026. During a long or thrashing agent run, watching your site disassemble itself in real time is the single most anxiety-producing thing in the shell, and there is currently no way to stop it. It is also the honest answer to Bolt's problem, where the documented failure mode is a preview stuck on 'Your preview will appear here'.

adopt.pattern: 'Board' mode — an infinite canvas of live page frames, for sites over ~6 pages
adopt.spec: A third option in the canvas chrome beside Preview and Code, labelled 'Board', auto-suggested (not auto-switched) once a project passes six pages via a one-time toast: 'Your site has 7 pages. Try Board to see them all at once.' Infinite pannable surface on #18181B; each page renders as a live iframe at 1280×800 scaled to fit, with a 1px zinc-800 frame, the page title above it at 12px/500 and the route beneath in mono 11px zinc-500. ⌘1 fit all, ⌘0 reset to 100%, space-drag to pan, scroll to zoom. Clicking a frame's title enters that page in Preview. Frames for pages not yet linked from anywhere get an amber 'Not linked from any page' chip — an orphan-page detector nobody else has.
adopt.rationale: Base44's Canvas (live-preview frames at desktop/tablet/phone, V/H/D/N/I, ⌘1 fit, ⌘0 100%) and Replit Agent 4's Design Canvas ('an infinite canvas that sits at the center of the design workflow') converged independently on this as the answer to 'show me my whole site'. Neither Lovable, Bolt, v0 nor Remixer has any multi-page overview at all — the shell simply has no representation of a site above the page level.

avoid.pattern: Two surfaces doing the same job in one navigation bar
avoid.why: GoDaddy Airo's six-item mode bar contains both 'Menu' ('Upload and insert images, videos or documents') and 'Media' ('Edit, upload and manage your app's visuals') — two asset managers, adjacent, in a six-item bar. A user cannot form a rule for which one to open. Any rail item we add must have a one-sentence job that no other item shares.

avoid.pattern: Letting the same control acquire two names
avoid.why: GoDaddy's own docs call one control 'Preview Desktop' in the build article and 'Change device' in the publish article, and the same share affordance is 'View & Share' in one place and 'Share link' in another. Label drift is the visible residue of a shell that was renamed and not fully updated — and it makes the help centre unusable. Lock control strings in a single source and let docs read from it.

avoid.pattern: Removing the credit balance from the shell
avoid.why: GoDaddy exiles it to User menu → 'Manage my plan' → 'Total AI Credit Usage'; a 2026 hands-on called it 'a nuisance' requiring constant navigation and listed it as a top complaint. Base44 hides it behind clicking the Base44 logo; Bolt puts it behind Profile → Subscription. Remixer's persistent top-toolbar credits chip is already best-in-class — the risk is that a future 'clean up the top bar' pass removes it. It stays.

avoid.pattern: Icon-only chrome with no accessible names
avoid.why: Querying every header button in v0's builder returns aria-label AND title null across the whole cluster (comments, preview, design mode, code, database) and the browser-chrome controls; only 'Add to favorites' carried a label. Icon-only controls without accessible names are unusable via screen reader and undiscoverable without hovering — an especially bad trade in a rail of 12+ glyphs.

avoid.pattern: Shipping a manual 'Refresh Preview' button
avoid.why: GoDaddy's build doc says '(Optional) If you don't see your edits updating, select Refresh Preview,' and its prompt best-practices table gives the recommended fix for 'Preview isn't working' as the prompt 'Restart dev server'. A user-facing refresh control is an admission that the preview desyncs, and 'dev server' is a developer concept leaking into a no-code product's official help text. Bolt has the same class of failure with previews stuck on 'Your preview will appear here'.

avoid.pattern: Modes that strip most of the shell
avoid.why: On a Base44 branch, publishing, secrets, connectors, automations, workflows, in-app agents, the code editor, theme settings, chat undo/edit and version-history restore are ALL disabled — while the branch still reads and writes live production data. A mode that removes ten capabilities is not a mode, it is a different product with the same chrome, and the user has no way to predict what will be missing.

avoid.pattern: Holding the shell hostage during generation
avoid.why: Wix Harmony shows a 'Don't leave this tab' modal mid-generation, warning that leaving the browser tab interrupts the build — turning a 4–7 minute wait into 4–7 minutes of enforced attention. Compare Lovable, where prompts sent during a run stack in a manipulable queue above the input, and Replit, where you can open a parallel planning chat while the main build runs.

avoid.pattern: Gating parts of the shell behind price tiers
avoid.why: Hostinger paywalls the code editor and file-structure view at Hobbyist $39.99/mo, so Explorer ($6.99) and Starter ($13.99) users cannot see part of their own shell and must spend a metered credit on every CSS tweak — reviewers note 'you can burn through 30 prompts in a single sitting'. Cheap tiers become structurally more expensive to use. Lovable makes the same mistake more mildly (Code editor read-only on Free).

avoid.pattern: Silently degrading the shell by browser or viewport
avoid.why: Bolt: 'Code view, project settings, and database access are unavailable on mobile devices,' and Safari code view is read-only with previews hosted rather than in-browser. Emergent's browser previews expire after 30 minutes. Base44's mobile app cuts visual edits, code, domains, security and templates. If a surface will be absent, the shell must say so where the control would have been — not leave a gap the user reads as a bug.

avoid.pattern: Version history that exists only inside the chat transcript
avoid.why: Figma Make has no file-level version history at all; 'versions' are builds you recover by scrolling the AI chat and clicking a 'Restore this version' icon, and a standing forum feature request exists asking for real history. Recovery is done under stress — it cannot require re-reading a conversation to find a state.

avoid.pattern: Configuration that exists only as a prompt you paste
avoid.why: GoDaddy's official contact-form article instructs users to paste literal strings into chat: 'CC [your email address here] to my email contact form' and 'Change my To email address to [your GoDaddy Conversations email here].' Settings reachable only by prompt are non-discoverable, brittle, and spend metered credits to change a value that should be a text field. Note the leak too — 'use the new email skill' exposes internal agent architecture in user-facing docs.

leapfrog.idea: Turn the centred domain switcher into the site's live control plane — a stateful 'public identity' chip, not a dropdown
leapfrog.spec: The centred top-bar chip shows the site's current public identity AND its state, using Remixer's existing colour rules: green dot + `acme.com` when live and in sync; amber dot + `acme.com · Draft changes`; indigo + `acme.remixer.app · Not connected'. Clicking opens a 420px popover with exactly three rows and nothing else. ADDRESS: the current URL with a pencil for the .remixer.app subdomain. DOMAIN: if none attached, an inline search field with placeholder 'Search for a domain' that buys in-flow; if attached, status plus SSL state. EMAIL: see the mailbox leapfrog. The row that no competitor can render: when the signed-in DreamHost account already holds a matching domain, the popover shows 'You already own acme.com' with a single 'Connect it' button and the end state is live in seconds with zero DNS steps, zero records shown, zero propagation warning.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: You only promote a control to permanent chrome when it resolves in seconds. For everyone else attaching a domain is a multi-vendor, multi-hour, may-fail operation — Bolt says 'up to 24 hours', Base44 says 'allow up to 48–72 hours' and sends users to whatsmydns.net, Figma makes you paste TXT and CNAME then press 'Refresh'. So they all bury domains in a settings page: Bolt at gear → All project settings → Domains & Hosting, Base44 at Dashboard → Domains, v0 at Publish → Customize. Even GoDaddy — the world's largest registrar — makes you leave the builder to godaddy.com/domains to buy and then come back.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost is the registrar of record. For a domain already in the user's DreamHost account there is no DNS work, no propagation window and no failure mode — which is the only condition under which a domain control earns permanent top-bar real estate. We already have the chip; we are currently spending it on a name instead of a state machine.

leapfrog.idea: 'Email' as a first-class rail item that provisions a real mailbox inside the build session
leapfrog.spec: Rail item 'Email', grouped under SHIP between Domains and Analytics. Empty state, verbatim: 'Your site has a contact form but no inbox. Create hello@acme.com — included in Remixer Build.' One field (the local part, prefilled 'hello'), one button 'Create mailbox'. On success the panel shows the address, storage used, and an 'Open webmail' link. Then wire it into the build narrative: when the agent generates a contact form, the chat step row reads 'Created contact form → delivers to hello@acme.com' rather than a generic sender, and the Forms panel shows submissions alongside the inbox they landed in. If the site has a form and no mailbox, the rail item carries an amber dot — the only amber in the rail — because that is a real broken loop, not a missing feature.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: It requires being an email host, and none of them are. Base44's docs state flatly 'Custom email domains are for sending only'; Lovable's say it 'does not provide mailboxes'; Bolt's entire domains documentation set (domains, connect, purchase, aliases, dns-records, ssl-https, troubleshoot) never mentions a mailbox — it will sell you a domain at checkout and leave you to buy Google Workspace; v0 has no email product at any tier. GoDaddy resells Microsoft 365 at $7.99/mo and its own comparison table concedes 'Professional email: Yes — Purchase required.' Only Hostinger bundles mailboxes, and it does so as a pricing-table ladder (0/1/2/5 per tier), never as a surface inside the builder shell.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost operates its own mail platform, so a mailbox is a provisioning call, not a reseller purchase — which means it can be a button in the rail rather than a link out to a storefront. It also closes the loop nobody else closes: every AI builder generates contact forms, and every one of them leaves the user with nowhere for the mail to go.

leapfrog.idea: Make the external-domain path a three-button shell state where 'Transfer to DreamHost' is the first option, not the last resort
leapfrog.spec: In the domain popover, an external domain surfaces three buttons in this priority order: (1) 'Transfer to DreamHost' — one-click start, framed as 'Move it here and we'll handle DNS forever'; (2) 'Auto-configure' — Entri or Domain Connect where the registrar supports it, so we sign in and write the records rather than showing them; (3) 'Enter records manually' — collapsed by default under a 'Do it yourself' disclosure. Every terminal state gets a verb, copying Lovable's state machine exactly: Verifying → button 'Check status'; Unable to verify → 'DNS verification didn't complete within one hour' + 'Retry'; Offline → 'Recover'; Removed → 'Reconnect'. Include the vendor-specific rescue line Lovable ships: for Cloudflare errors, 'Set this record to DNS only (grey cloud), not Proxied.' All of it renders inside the top-bar popover — the user never leaves the canvas.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Everyone else's incentive stops at 'connected'. They cannot offer a transfer because they are not the registrar (Bolt resells, likely via Name.com, with a 60-day lock; Emergent resells IONOS; Base44 resells Wix or IONOS), so the best they can do is automate record-writing. Replit — not a registrar at all — bought the capability off the shelf: its docs describe 'automated DNS configuration using Entri, a third-party service that can sign into your registrar and write records on your behalf, bypassing manual entry', with a 5 June 2026 release note reading 'Custom domain DNS setup automated'. That is the bar we are currently below, given DreamHost has no Domain Connect as of Aug 2026.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: We are the only player for whom 'transfer it to us' is both a legitimate first suggestion and a permanent fix — it converts every future domain interaction into the zero-DNS path, and it moves the registration revenue onto our own books. Nobody else can put a button in their builder that makes the DNS problem never happen again.

leapfrog.idea: A property board, not a page board — pages in the centre, owned infrastructure orbiting them as live cards
leapfrog.spec: Extend Board mode beyond page frames. Pages sit centre on the infinite canvas; connected services render as 220×120 live cards around them, each with a green/amber state dot: 'acme.com — Live · SSL valid · 10 PoPs'; 'hello@acme.com — 3 unread'; 'Contact form — 12 submissions this week'; 'SmartEdge — 220ms p50, 4 regions'; 'Database — 3 tables, 214 rows'. Draw real 1px zinc-700 curves from the contact-form card to the mailbox card, and from the domain card to the pages, because those are actual data paths we own both ends of. Clicking any card opens the matching rail panel. Amber on any card means one specific broken loop with one specific verb — 'Form has no inbox → Create mailbox', 'Domain not connected → Connect'.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Base44's Canvas and Replit's Design Canvas both render page frames, and both stop there, because a page board is all they own.
