Drawing an arrow from a contact form to a mailbox requires operating the form, the mail transport and the inbox; drawing a CDN latency card requires operating the edge. Lovable rents Supabase-derived Cloud and sends outbound mail with no inboxes; Bolt rents Cloudflare and Render-class hosting; v0 hands operations to the Vercel dashboard; Base44 apps resolve to base44.onrender.com and send via SendGrid.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost owns the registrar, DNS, the mailbox, SmartEdge's 10 PoPs and the logs — every endpoint of every arrow. This is the only view in the category that can show a user their whole web property, not just their pages, and it turns the rail from a list of tools into a diagram of a running business.

leapfrog.idea: Make publishing free, label every free surface, and say it in the shell
leapfrog.spec: Remove credit consumption from publishing entirely. Then adopt GoDaddy's discipline of publishing the free list, but put it in the product rather than a help article: a small zinc-600 11px 'Free' tag on the Publish button's tooltip, on the version-history Restore button, on the Board and Preview toggles, and on direct visual edits. Copy in the credits chip popover, verbatim: 'Credits are used when Remixer's AI builds or edits. Publishing, hosting, SSL, your domain, your mailbox and restoring a version are always free.' Pair it with Figma Make's staging mechanic for the visual editor — direct manipulations accumulate in the composer as a reviewable batch, credit-free, until the user applies them.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: They cannot afford to draw the line where we can, because they are reselling inference and renting their edge — so the meter has to reach further into the shell. Even so, every one of them has drawn a free line somewhere and Remixer's is in the worst place in the category: Lovable states 'Publishing itself is free' and gives 100 free inline text edits per user per day; Bolt charges no tokens for version restores, UI-button actions or security audits; Base44 exempts manual visual edits and all database reads/writes; GoDaddy publishes an explicit no-credit list covering Preview, Code, Edit, Media and History restore; Figma Make stages visual edits credit-free until applied.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost owns SmartEdge, the CDN, the DNS and the hosting, so the marginal cost of a publish is near zero — we are currently charging credits for the one operation whose cost we already absorbed. Making publishing free is not a discount, it is correcting a mispriced surface, and it lets us say the sentence no token-reseller can: shipping is free here.

open_questions: What is actually in Remixer's right icon rail today — the exact items, their order, and whether each has an aria-label and a tooltip? The brief specifies the rail exists but not its contents, and I could not audit it. The lifecycle-grouping recommendation cannot be specced further without that inventory.

Does Remixer have any keyboard shortcuts today, and is ⌘K unclaimed across our supported browsers and common extensions? If we ship a palette, does it index only the current project or projects-plus-settings the way Lovable's does?
Is the ~408px chat panel currently resizable or collapsible at all? What is the minimum usable canvas width at 1280 and 1440, and does that put a hard floor under the resize range?

Where does version history live in Remixer's shell today — top bar, rail, or inside the chat thread? Bolt deliberately promoted it from a title menu into the top nav in July 2026; we should know which side of that move we are on.

Is 'publishing burns credits' a pricing decision or a technical one? Given we own SmartEdge, the CDN, DNS and SSL, what is the actual marginal cost of a publish, and what would removing the charge cost in modelled revenue versus retained users?
Does the model layer support per-file or per-page scoping at all? Lock and Focus are cheap in the UI and expensive in the agent if the context assembly has no notion of an excluded path.

Domain Connect: build or buy? Replit shipped automated external-registrar DNS via Entri on 5 June 2026 without being a registrar. What is our timeline, and should 'Transfer to DreamHost' outrank 'Auto-configure' in the popover given our economics?

Can a mailbox be provisioned via API from inside a builder session, or does it require a DreamHost panel round trip? That single answer decides whether Email is a button in the rail or a link out — and a link out puts us level with GoDaddy rather than ahead of it.

What is our page-count and file-count ceiling, and where does the builder start to degrade? Base44 publishes 600 pages and warns that total file count and source size matter more. We need our own number before we design a page switcher for it.

What is our mobile shell? Every native builder app in the field (Lovable, Base44, Replit, v0) collapses to chat plus preview and cuts visual editing, code and settings. Do we ship responsive web, a native app, or explicitly nothing — and if responsive web, which rail items survive?
Does the centred domain switcher currently render state (live / draft changes / not connected) or only a name? Everything in the leapfrog depends on it being a state machine.
Do we have a canonical string registry for UI labels? GoDaddy's shell has the same control named two ways across its own docs; we should confirm we cannot drift the same way as the rail grows.

lens: The chat/agent editing model — how an edit request becomes a visible change, and what happens when the AI is wrong
executive_take:
The chat/agent editing model has stopped being an argument about generation quality and become an argument about the economics and legibility of the loop AFTER generation. Five patterns now define the state of the art, and no single product has all five.

(1) Two-speed modes with asymmetric pricing. Lovable's Plan mode is a flat 1 credit and never touches code; Base44's Discuss is a flat 0.3 against 0.5–4 for execution; Bolt's "Plan" pill sits beside "Build now" on the landing page itself, before the first prompt. Thinking is cheap, doing is metered.

(2) A free direct-manipulation lane. Base44 docs: manual visual edits "do not consume credits." Replit's Element Editor writes text, font size/weight, alignment, colour, margin and padding straight to source with no agent call and no credits. Lovable gives 100 free inline text edits per user per day. GoDaddy publishes a no-credit action list and actively steers users away from chat: "Use Edit instead of typing a prompt… It's free."

(3) Staged, reviewable commits. Figma Make (30 Jul 2026) stages every direct manipulation in the prompt box "staged and credit-free, until you apply them" — one Apply spends credits and cuts one version.

(4) Visual self-QA. v0 loads a headless browser, screenshots its own page at desktop AND mobile, posts both into chat, diagnoses a real defect ("the Button component doesn't support asChild") and repairs it. Replit Agent 3 shows the agent's own cursor clicking around inside the Agent pane.

(5) Addressable, honest history. Base44 puts a Revert icon on every chat message; Lovable adds Bookmarks, a "Published" badge on the live version, per-version diffs, and a disabled-state tooltip: "Cannot revert this far back in history."

The real gap: nobody has solved DATA. Lovable, Bolt and Base44 all state plainly that revert does not roll back the database; Base44's branches "read/write identical records" while being sold as safe experiments; point-in-time data history is paywalled at $160/mo (Base44 Elite) and $95/mo (Replit Pro). And nobody shows cost before you spend — Bolt's own reviewers: "it is not always clear what a given action will cost before you run it."

Remixer's honest position: fastest generation in the field (2–3 min vs v0's measured 6m21s, Bolt's documented ~5, Base44's 3–5, Wix Harmony's 4–7, Emergent's ~10), the longest no-card trial, 1,000 credits/mo, and a persistent credits chip GoDaddy conspicuously lacks. But we bill credits for PUBLISHING — a behaviour I could not find documented at any competitor — and we have no plan mode, per-turn checkpoint, blast-radius lock, free-edit lane or self-QA loop. We are ahead on the funnel and behind on the loop.

comparison.approach: Build/Plan modes toggled with Option+P; Plan is a flat 1 credit and renders a full-screen editable markdown plan with highlight-to-revise ("Describe the change…") and a strikethrough/highlight diff behind "Show changes"/"Edit plan". Build shows activity cards naming each step and file, plus expandable subagent rows ("Explore: How does the current authentication flow work?"). Queued prompts form a manipulable stack above the input (pause, reorder, edit, repeat up to 50x). Every message's three-dot menu shows cost, duration and a shareable permalink. Automatic versioning with Bookmarks tab, a "Published" badge on the live version, per-version diff and Revert. Preview toolbar: S select / T inline text / D draw annotation / C comment, draggable, position remembered. "Try to fix" on error cards is free within fair use; first 100 inline text edits per user per day are free.
comparison.notes: The only product that has designed the whole loop: cheap negotiation, legible execution, addressable history, honest failure, free recovery. Weakness — fine-grained visual edits get silently overwritten by later prompts (Superblocks), and Revert explicitly "does not restore or roll back your database data."

comparison.approach: No plan mode. Instead: the agent declares an art direction out loud ("I'll commit to a warm, editorial craft-coffee direction with a deep espresso palette and amber accents"), writes theme colours and font tokens BEFORE components, then loads an "agent-browser skill", screenshots its own output at desktop and mobile, posts both thumbnails into chat, self-diagnoses a real bug, fixes all four call sites, and chases a false-positive console error to ground. Step rows are semantic and past-tense with queued work pre-dimmed three at a time. Design Mode adds a property inspector with Undo/Redo/Reset, a Before/After toggle, Cmd+I to switch between inspect and interact, and auto-attaches a screenshot of the selected element to any natural-language instruction. Apply batches edits into a real chat version. Forking from a specific version is a first-class primitive with a public API endpoint.
comparison.notes: Best self-QA loop in the category by a distance — but the self-healing is billable under raw token metering, and in my measured anonymous run roughly a third of the 6m21s was spent fixing an incompatibility in v0's OWN starter Button component.

comparison.approach: Three modes — Default (acts instantly), Discuss (flat 0.3 credits, plans safely), Edit (click elements in preview) — switched with Cmd+. / Ctrl+. "even while you're typing a prompt." Queue up to 7 messages. Custom Instructions (always-on) and Freeze Files ("Lock specific files or entities so the AI does not modify them"). Per-message Revert icon plus a clock-icon Version History. Edit-mode toolbar exposes real tokens including a raw Tailwind Classes field; manual visual edits cost zero credits. AI diffs are opt-in behind a message hover menu → "View Changes" with a colour-coded file tree and side-by-side view. "Redesign this in different styles" returns four options side by side with previews "before it touches anything."
comparison.notes: Cmd+. mid-typing and the per-message Revert icon are the two best small details in the field. Undermined by branches that share live production data, "Credits are non-refundable for tool behavior and AI mistakes", and raw Python stack traces ("'dict' object has no attribute 'lower'") leaking to a no-code audience.

comparison.approach: Agent modes surfaced as a cost/quality dial: Lite / Economy / Power, plus a Turbo advanced setting for "up to 2.5x faster builds at higher cost." Agent 3 runs autonomously up to 200 minutes with a "Max Autonomy (Beta)" toggle in the Agent Tools section of the input box, and App Testing opens a real browser inside the Agent pane "showing the Agent's cursor as it clicks around." Agent creates checkpoints as it works. Element Editor makes a defined edit set (text, font size/weight, alignment, text and background colour, margin, padding) free by writing source directly, escalating to Agent only when scope exceeds that. Agent 4 adds an infinite Design Canvas, a parallel planning chat while the main build runs, and a shared Kanban (Drafts / Active / Ready / Done).
comparison.notes: The published free/paid boundary drawn at "does this need the model" is the most defensible in the category. Wrecked by effort-based billing opacity — The Register (18 Sept 2025) reported surprise overruns; one user burned $70 in a night against a $100–250/month norm.

comparison.approach: Plan mode via "/plan" produces a real plan.md that opens automatically and can be edited directly, with "no limit to how many times you can refine before approving" and a "Build" button in chat. The 30 Jul 2026 properties panel exposes a DOM tree plus spacing, typography, layout, opacity, z-index, radius and codebase-bound tokens — and every direct manipulation "stages every edit in the prompt box so you can review each change before you commit to it, or discard anything that doesn't look right", staying credit-free until Apply. "Annotate for agent" drops numbered blue callouts to bind vague intent to a precise target ("make this section feel calmer").
comparison.notes: The staging model is the single best answer to credit anxiety anywhere in this field. Fatally undercut by having NO file-level version history — "versions" are just builds you scroll back to in the chat — and plan mode costing MORE credits than build mode.

comparison.approach: Plan Mode is a composer pill that "highlights blue when active" and terminates in quick-action buttons ("Implement this plan", "Show an example", "Refine this idea") that auto-switch back to Build. Right-clicking files gives "Target file", "Lock file", "Lock all" under the heading "Guide Bolt's focus" — user-controllable blast radius. Highlighting code raises "Ask Bolt" which links the selection into the prompt. Version history is a bookmarkable, renameable timeline with preview-before-restore; restores cost no tokens and are marketed as the cheap alternative to prompting an undo. GitHub auto-commits only on changes "that doesn't break the project."
comparison.notes: Best blast-radius control in the field and the smartest commit heuristic. But there is NO documented one-click fix button — recovery is reading the Terminal tab or opening the browser console ("On macOS: press CMD + Option + J"), error loops bill at full price, and cost scales with project size rather than intent.

comparison.approach: "Design Variations" (mid-July 2026, free): one click produces five complete alternative directions — layout, colour, typography — previewed and applied "rather than re-prompting from scratch." Annotation mode lets you draw directly on the running app in the preview window. Prompt box carries an "I'm Feeling Lucky" generator and typed capability chips (image generation, Maps data). API keys are injected server-side and never appear in client code.
comparison.notes: Design Variations is the cheapest known kill for the aesthetic re-prompting loop and it is free. But there is no documented checkpoint, diff, revert or error-recovery model at all — the editing loop is one-directional.

comparison.approach: Generation renders as a clickable numbered build-plan queue in chat; clicking a step runs it, clicking its number opens an explanation. The agent validates its own code post-build and repairs errors without consuming credits; runtime failures raise a one-click "Ask Airo to Fix It". Recovery is two-layer: History (under the chat window, "Restore this version", preview before restoring) and Backups (files, databases, or both, by date). Both restore paths end with "Once restored, select Publish to make it live" — restore never auto-publishes. Docs actively steer users away from chat: "Use Edit for simple edits… It's free, and Airo AI Builder can't make unintended changes when you're editing directly."
comparison.notes: Strong recovery philosophy, worst editing legibility: no inline diffs, no file chips, no per-message revert, no mode toggle, credit balance exiled to Manage-my-plan (reviewers call it "a nuisance"), and configuration done by pasting GoDaddy-authored prompt strings into chat — which spends credits to change a setting.

comparison.approach: "Select and edit" scopes the NEXT prompt to a clicked element; a separate "Edit Content" mode edits static text and images directly with no AI. Clarifying questions come with clickable answer options plus free-text fallback. Undo is a curved-arrow icon under the last message; Restore sits under any earlier message. Chat panel is drag-resizable with persisted width, drag-to-hide, double-click reset.
comparison.notes: Two genuinely good mechanisms (scope-the-prompt vs bypass-the-AI as separate tools; the three-behaviour resize handle). Ruined by destructive recovery — Undo "permanently deletes" the message and response, Restore warns "All your messages after this message will be permanently deleted", and neither "reinstate[s] credits spent on the reverted messages" — plus a code editor paywalled at $39.99 that forces every CSS tweak through paid credits on cheap tiers.

comparison.approach: Left AI chat panel (~408px), centre canvas/preview, right icon rail, Visual Editor, dark #18181B shell with a persistent credits chip in the top toolbar. Credits are consumed by generation, chat edits AND publishing changes. 1,000 credits/mo + 1,000 bonus first month; 30-day no-card trial; 2–3 min first generation. No documented plan/discuss mode, no per-turn checkpoint or per-message revert, no blast-radius lock, no free direct-manipulation lane, no self-QA loop, no per-message cost disclosure, no staged-edit commit.
comparison.notes: Ahead of the field on the funnel (fastest generation, longest no-card trial, persistent credits chip) and behind on the loop. The publish-burns-credits behaviour is a category outlier I could not find at any competitor — Lovable states publishing is free, GoDaddy's published no-credit action list covers restore and non-AI edits, Bolt bills tokens only for agent work.

best_in_class.why: It is the only product in the field that has designed all five stages of the loop rather than two or three. (1) Negotiation is cheap and structured: Plan mode is a flat 1 credit, renders as an editable full-screen document, and lets you select any passage to open "Describe the change…", with revisions shown as struck-through old wording and highlighted new wording behind a "Show changes"/"Edit plan" toggle — the review affordance every knowledge worker already knows from Docs. (2) Execution is legible: activity cards name the step, the files and the tool, and subagent rows expose parallel read-only investigation with human-readable titles. (3) The wait is productive: queued prompts form a manipulable stack above the input that can be paused, reordered, edited and repeated up to 50 times, which also kills the "did my message get lost?" failure. (4) History is addressable and honest: automatic versioning, a Bookmarks tab, a "Published" badge marking the live version so version history doubles as the deploy ledger, per-version diffs, and — critically — a Revert that is disabled with the tooltip "Cannot revert this far back in history" rather than failing silently, plus a plain statement that it "does not restore or roll back your database data." (5) Recovery is free by policy and the policy is stated: "Try to fix" on error cards, "Try to fix all" on security findings, both scan types, design-system verification turns, and the first 100 inline text edits per user per day are all billed at zero credits. No competitor refuses to charge for cleaning up its own mess this systematically. v0 has the better self-QA and Figma Make has the better free/paid boundary, but neither has a plan mode plus an addressable history plus a free recovery policy at the same time.

adopt.pattern: Stop charging credits to publish — and merchandise that fact
adopt.spec: Remove credit consumption from publish and republish entirely. Publish button (top-right, blue #1587FF) gains a 6px amber dot when the live version is stale — one signal, mirrored by a "Live" badge on the corresponding row in version history. The publish dialog's first line reads: "Publishing is free. Credits are only spent when the AI builds or edits." The credits chip in the top toolbar gains a popover with a "What's free" section listing, verbatim: Preview · Manual visual edits · Uploading images and files · Restoring a version · Publishing and republishing · Fixing our own mistakes.
adopt.rationale: Publishing-burns-credits is a category outlier I could not find documented at any competitor. Lovable states plainly: "Publishing itself is free. Only backend activity… consumes Run credits. A live site with no backend activity incurs no credit charges." GoDaddy publishes a no-credit action list covering preview, code, non-AI edits, media upload and History restore, and publish appears nowhere on its billable list. Bolt bills tokens only for agent work and makes version restores and UI-button actions free. Taxing the single moment of success is the most resentment-generating placement available, and it is the first thing a competitor comparison page will attack.

adopt.pattern: Plan mode: a flat-priced, editable plan with a strikethrough diff and a Build handoff
adopt.spec: Add a mode chip in the composer, immediately left of the send button, reading "Build ⌄" by default and "Plan" when toggled; Alt+P / Option+P switches it and works mid-typing. In Plan the chip fills with the Remixer indigo/purple AI gradient and carries a trailing microlabel "1 credit". Plan responses open full-height in the centre canvas as an editable markdown document with fixed sections: Overview · Pages · Data & forms · What I'll build first. Selecting any passage raises a popover input placeholdered "Describe the change…". Revisions render old wording struck through and new wording highlighted, toggled by a segmented control top-right reading "Show changes | Edit plan". Primary button, bottom-right: "Build this plan" — which switches the composer back to Build and starts execution.
adopt.rationale: Three of the five majors ship this and price it deliberately: Lovable's Plan is a flat 1 credit and "never touches code"; Base44's Discuss is a flat 0.3 against 0.5–4 for execution; Bolt's Plan pill "highlights blue when active" and appears on the landing page before the first prompt. It is simultaneously the cheapest possible undo (nothing was built), a credit-saving mechanism users feel in control of, and a reframe from slot machine to collaborator. Base44's Cmd+. that works "even while you're typing a prompt" is the specific detail to copy — intent changes mid-sentence.

adopt.pattern: A free direct-manipulation lane with a visible boundary and automatic escalation
adopt.spec: In the Visual Editor define an explicit Free Edit set — text content, font family/size/weight, text alignment, text colour, background colour, per-side padding and margin, corner radius, opacity — written straight to source with no model call. The element toolbar shows a small green "Free" pill while every selected control is inside that set. Any control outside it renders in the AI indigo with a hover label "Ask AI — about 0.5 credits". Independently, the first 100 inline text edits per user per day are free regardless of mechanism. Empty-state hint the first time a user selects an element: "Nudging, retyping and recolouring are free. Save credits for the big changes."
adopt.rationale: Base44's docs exempt "manual visual edits (dragging, layout changes, direct text editing)" from credits entirely. Replit's Element Editor names the identical free set (text, font size/weight, alignment, text colour, background colour, margin, padding) and "seamlessly sends targeted metadata to Agent" only when scope exceeds it. Lovable gives 100 free inline text edits per user per day specifically so nobody is ever charged to fix a typo. GoDaddy goes furthest and tells users to avoid its own AI: "Use Edit for simple edits… It's free, and Airo AI Builder can't make unintended changes when you're editing directly." The paid boundary should be "does this need the model", not "is this an edit".

adopt.pattern: Staged edits: batch direct manipulations into the composer, commit with one Apply
adopt.spec: Every Visual Editor change stacks as a chip in a tray directly above the composer: "Hero padding 32 → 48 ×", "H1 colour → #1E1E24 ×". Tray footer reads "4 staged changes" on the left and a filled button "Apply" on the right; a text link "Discard all" sits between them. Apply writes all staged changes in a single commit and cuts exactly one version. If any staged change falls outside the Free Edit set, the button reads "Apply (1 needs AI · ~0.5 cr)". Nothing in the tray costs anything until Apply is pressed.
adopt.rationale: Figma Make shipped exactly this on 30 July 2026: direct manipulations "stage every edit in the prompt box so you can review each change before you commit to it, or discard anything that doesn't look right", accumulating "staged and credit-free, until you apply them." It converts the composer from a command line into a review queue, makes the spend feel deliberate rather than extracted, and — because it commits once — it stops the version history filling with 40 one-pixel checkpoints.

adopt.pattern: A Revert icon on every AI turn, and a Restore that never auto-publishes
adopt.spec: Each completed assistant message gets a hover action row on its footer: "↩ Revert to here · Copy · 0.6 cr · 41s". "Revert to here" restores the project to the state immediately before that turn and posts a system line in the transcript: "Reverted to before 'Add a booking form'. Your live site hasn't changed — publish to make this live." When revert is impossible the control is disabled with tooltip "Can't revert this far back". Separately, a clock icon at the top of the chat panel opens full version history with a Bookmarks tab, a "Live" badge on the currently published version, and preview-before-restore on every row.
adopt.rationale: Base44 attaches a Revert icon to every chat message, mapping undo onto the unit users actually think in — "that thing I asked for" — rather than onto files or timestamps. Lovable pairs per-message "Revert to this version" with a Bookmarks tab, a "Published" badge that turns version history into a deploy ledger, and an honest disabled tooltip. GoDaddy gets the decoupling right: both its restore paths end "Once restored, select Publish to make it live", so a panicked rollback is previewable and reversible before the public sees anything. Base44 also warns that asking the AI in chat to undo "never actually undoes prompt changes" — the control must be a button, not a sentence.

adopt.pattern: Blast-radius locks: "Don't touch this page"
adopt.spec: Right-click any page or component in the pages list to open a context menu headed "Guide the AI's focus" containing: "Focus AI here" (inserts a dismissible chip into the composer reading "Focused: Pricing ×" and scopes the next turns), "Lock page" and "Lock all" (excluded from AI edits; a small padlock renders beside the page name in the page dropdown and in the canvas breadcrumb). Locked pages that an AI turn wanted to touch produce a chat line: "Skipped Pricing — it's locked. Unlock it?" with an inline Unlock button.
adopt.rationale: Bolt ships this as "Target file" / "Lock file" / "Lock all" under the literal heading "Guide Bolt's focus", with the rationale "You'll get more accurate results if you're explicit about what Bolt should and shouldn't change." Base44 ships the same idea as "Freeze Files: Lock specific files or entities so the AI does not modify them." One context menu answers three separate complaints at once — the AI changed something I didn't ask about, it hallucinated across unrelated pages, and it burned my credits re-reading everything. Critically, this is also the fix for the documented Lovable failure where "fine-grained design edits can be overwritten by subsequent prompts" because visual and chat edits write the same files with no protected-region concept.

adopt.pattern: Visual self-QA: the agent checks its own work and posts desktop + mobile proof, then offers a free fix
adopt.spec: After every build turn that changes layout, the agent renders the affected page headlessly at 1440px and 390px, posts two thumbnails side by side in the chat under a step row reading "Checked it in a browser", and states what it verified in one sentence. If it finds a runtime error it posts an error card with the error in plain language and a single primary button: "Fix it — free". Under the button, in 12px secondary text: "Fixing our own mistakes never costs credits." Step rows throughout use semantic past-tense labels ("Set the colour theme", "Built the booking form", "Checked it in a browser") not file paths, with the next three queued steps rendered pre-dimmed.
adopt.rationale: v0 does exactly this — loads an agent-browser skill, screenshots desktop and mobile, posts both into chat, then narrates a real diagnosis and fix. Replit Agent 3 goes further and shows the agent's own cursor clicking around inside the Agent pane. Both convert dead waiting time into the single most trust-building moment in the product. The free-fix half is Lovable's: "Try to fix" and "Try to fix all" are billed at zero credits, and this is the specific antidote to the loudest complaint in the entire field — Bolt users reporting 7–12M tokens burned in an afternoon on error loops, Base44's blunt "Credits are non-refundable for tool behavior and AI mistakes", and v0 users saying "we are literally paying for all the good/bad codes that v0 generates."

adopt.pattern: Per-message cost, duration, and a session running-total in the credits popover
adopt.spec: The hover row on each completed AI message shows "0.6 cr · 41s" inline, with a three-dot menu offering Copy, Copy link, and Rate. Keep the credits chip exactly where it is in the top toolbar; add a popover containing four blocks: (1) "842 of 1,000 credits left · resets 1 Sep"; (2) "This session: 4.2 credits"; (3) the "What's free" list; (4) one line of spend policy — "We spend credits closest to expiry first, free ones before paid."
adopt.rationale: Lovable is the only product that surfaces per-message cost, and it does so at the point of consumption via a three-dot menu showing cost, duration and a shareable link. Bolt's reviewers name the absence as the core wound: "it is not always clear what a given action will cost before you run it." GoDaddy exiles the balance to a separate Manage-my-plan page and reviewers call it "a nuisance" — so our persistent chip is already ahead and should be extended, not moved. GoDaddy's published expiry-first spend order ("starting with those expiring soonest… includes both free and paid credits") is worth stating in one line because it removes the "am I burning the credits I paid for?" anxiety.

adopt.pattern: Three named design directions before any code, free, and skipped for app-shaped prompts
adopt.spec: When the first prompt is visually open-ended, render three direction cards in the canvas instead of building. Each card: a live thumbnail, a name ("Warm editorial", "Clean utility", "Bold display"), the font pairing in words, and three hex swatches. Below them a single input placeholdered "Refine this direction…" and a primary button "Build this one". Costs 0 credits; only the chosen direction triggers the metered build. Skip the step entirely — build immediately — when the prompt describes a dashboard, admin tool, internal app, or a URL to clone.
adopt.rationale: Lovable generates three parallel HTML/Tailwind design directions for open-ended prompts with up to six refinements, and explicitly SKIPS the step for dashboards, admin tools and cloned URLs where users want speed not art direction. Base44's Design Pack returns four options side by side and states "AI shows previews before it touches anything." Google AI Studio's Design Variations returns five, in one click, free. This is the strongest anti-generic-output mechanism in the field and it also kills the aesthetic re-prompting loop, which is the single most credit-wasteful user behaviour in every metered builder.

adopt.pattern: A manipulable message queue above the composer
adopt.spec: Prompts sent while the agent is working stack above the composer as rows with a drag handle, the prompt text truncated to one line, and edit / × controls. A header row reads "Queued — will run in order" with a "Pause queue" text button on the right. Paused rows dim. Maximum 7 queued.
adopt.rationale: Lovable puts queued prompts in "a visible queue above the chat input" that can be paused, reordered, edited, copied, removed and repeated up to 50 times; Base44 caps at 7 ("You can queue up to 7 messages at once"). It converts multi-minute agent waits from anxious dead time into a planning surface and eliminates the "did my message get lost?" failure mode entirely. Cheap to build relative to everything else on this list.

avoid.pattern: Billing users for the AI's own mistakes and error loops
avoid.why: This is the loudest complaint in the entire category and it is quantified. Bolt Product Hunt: "it's unfortunate that they still get consumed when there's errors because solving the errors can take quite a while"; reviewers estimate up to half their tokens went to errors, with reports of 7–12 million tokens in an afternoon and 20M+ on a single authentication issue. Base44 states the policy outright — "Credits are non-refundable for tool behavior and AI mistakes" — and reviewers describe the AI getting "stuck on a feature, retries multiple times, and burns through credits without making progress." v0's community thread "Credits are burning way too fast" contains "We are literally paying for all the good/bad codes that v0 generates, it's terrible", with one user measuring ~20% of iterations as corrections for v0-caused breakage. In my own anonymous v0 run, roughly a third of the 6m21s build was spent fixing an incompatibility in v0's own starter Button component. Lovable and GoDaddy both chose the opposite policy and it is their most-praised decision.

avoid.pattern: Destructive undo that deletes forward history and refunds nothing
avoid.why: Hostinger Horizons: the Undo control means "your last message and the Horizon's corresponding response are permanently deleted"; Restore confirms with "All your messages after this message will be permanently deleted"; and docs state "Undoing or restoring a version does not cost additional credits and does not reinstate credits spent on the reverted messages." A linear destructive history means recovery is itself a risk, so users stop using it. Lovable's model is the counter-example — chat history and later edits survive a revert so changes can be reapplied.

avoid.pattern: Revert that silently doesn't roll back data, or a 'safe' branch that writes to production
avoid.why: Lovable: reverting "does not restore or roll back your database data." Bolt: "Restoring to an earlier project version will not change your current Bolt or Supabase databases" — with no warning documented in the restore confirmation flow. Base44 is worse: branches shipped Aug 2026 marketed as "Branch your app to try changes safely", but docs confirm branches share "Live app data (all branches read/write identical records)." A non-technical user who believes undo is complete can corrupt production records from what they were told was an experiment. If we cannot roll data back, the revert dialog must say so in the dialog, not in a docs page.

avoid.pattern: Hiding the credit balance on a separate page
avoid.why: GoDaddy requires User menu → "Manage my plan" → "Total AI Credit Usage" to see a balance. A 2026 hands-on: "unlike other AI builders that display a running tally of your AI credit use somewhere on the dashboard, GoDaddy keeps Airo's tucked away on a separate screen" — described as "a nuisance" requiring constant navigation, and listed among the reviewer's top complaints. Remixer's persistent top-toolbar chip is already the better pattern; the risk is regressing it, not adopting it.

avoid.pattern: Configuration by pasted prompt instead of a settings control
avoid.why: GoDaddy's official contact-form help article instructs users to paste literal strings into chat: "Can we update our contact form and use the new email skill to see if we need to make any changes?", "CC [your email address here] to my email contact form", "Change my To email address to [your GoDaddy Conversations email here]." This is brittle, non-discoverable, leaks internal architecture ("email skill") to end users, and spends metered credits to change a setting. Anything with a finite set of valid values wants a control, not a sentence.

avoid.pattern: Leaking developer internals into the recovery path
avoid.why: GoDaddy's own prompt best-practices table lists, for "Preview isn't working", the recommended user prompt "Restart dev server" — a dev-server concept surfaced as the official remedy in a no-code product. Base44's troubleshooting doc enumerates errors real users see including "Failed to load app: Error serializing to JSON: UnicodeEncodeError" (triggered by characters in an app NAME) and "'dict' object has no attribute 'lower'" — a raw Python AttributeError shown to someone sold no-code. Bolt outsources debugging entirely: "On macOS: press CMD + Option + J." Each of these is a hard stop for the exact persona these products market to.

avoid.pattern: Letting later chat turns silently overwrite careful manual visual edits
avoid.why: Superblocks' hands-on of Lovable documents that "fine-grained design edits can be overwritten by subsequent prompts", because visual edits and chat edits write to the same files with no lock or protected-region concept. The user experiences this as the AI undoing their work at random, which destroys trust in both surfaces at once. This is precisely why Bolt's Lock file and Base44's Freeze Files exist — a free direct-manipulation lane is worthless if the manipulations aren't durable.

avoid.pattern: Publishing a thrift manual instead of fixing the pricing
avoid.why: Bolt maintains an official guide, "Maximizing token efficiency", teaching users to avoid its own meter: use Plan mode, use UI buttons ("doesn't consume tokens"), "Use Version History to undo changes without tokens", "Clear context", "Turn on connectors only when you need them", "Avoid repeated automated error fix attempts." GoDaddy frames prompt quality the same way: "'Fix my site' costs more credits than 'The checkout button isn't processing payments…'". Naming which actions are FREE is excellent; needing a strategy guide for not spending money is an admission the model is hostile, and it keeps the meter permanently in the user's foreground — the opposite of the flow state a builder wants.

avoid.pattern: Blocking the user's browser tab during generation
avoid.why: Wix Harmony surfaces a "Don't leave this tab" modal mid-generation warning that leaving would interrupt the build. Reviewers flag it as a genuine constraint for anyone who tab-switches. It converts a 5-minute wait into 5 minutes of enforced attention, and it is a hard admission that the build is client-tethered. Lovable's opposite handling is the model: an idle preview degrades to "Still building?" with a "Keep building" button, and docs stress it "does not affect the published app or project data."

leapfrog.idea: Paired rollback: undo that restores the database as well as the code — free, on every plan
leapfrog.spec: Every AI turn that touches the schema or writes data cuts a paired snapshot: code version + database point-in-time marker. The per-message "Revert to here" dialog then shows two pre-checked rows with real counts: "☑ Restore the site (7 files)" and "☑ Restore your data — rolls back to 4:12 PM · 12 rows change, 0 rows deleted". Unchecking the data row is allowed and the button label updates to "Restore site only". After reverting, the transcript posts: "Reverted to before 'Add a booking form'. Your live site hasn't changed — publish to make this live." Retention: 30 days, all plans, zero credits. Surface it in version history as a small database glyph on any row that carries a data snapshot.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Because the pure-AI builders rent their backends and cannot offer point-in-time recovery cheaply. Lovable states revert "does not restore or roll back your database data"; Bolt states "Restoring to an earlier project version will not change your current Bolt or Supabase databases"; Base44's branches "read/write identical records" against production. Where it exists at all it is a premium hostage: Base44 gates 7-day entity version history at Elite ($160/mo, shipped 1 Aug 2026) and Replit gates 28-day database rollbacks at Pro ($95/mo). Nobody gives it away at $9.99 because nobody else owns the storage layer.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost already operates the database, the storage and a backup pipeline as its core hosting business. Point-in-time snapshots are a solved operational problem for us and a rented, metered upstream cost for Lovable, Bolt, Base44 and v0. Shipping the one thing the whole category explicitly disclaims — at the price where competitors disclaim it — is the cleanest possible proof that "built by a host" means something.

leapfrog.idea: Roll back the launch, not just the build — publish history that reverts the deployed site, the CDN and the DNS together
leapfrog.spec: Add a "Live" tab beside History in the chat panel. Each row is one publish: timestamp, version label, a one-line summary of what changed, and — where relevant — badges for "domain connected", "DNS changed", "SSL issued". Every row carries "Roll back live site", which restores the deployed snapshot, purges SmartEdge across all 10 PoPs, and, when that publish also altered the connected domain or its records, offers a second checkbox: "☑ Also restore DNS records (3 changes)" with the records listed inline. Confirmation copy: "Visitors will see the previous version within about 30 seconds." Every publish is also automatically bookmarkable so a user can pin a known-good launch.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Restoring a build is easy; restoring the route to it requires holding the zone. Lovable, Bolt, v0 and Base44 can all revert code but none can touch DNS — Lovable's whole domain surface is a state machine of Verifying/Stalled/Offline/Removed with recovery verbs, not a history you can roll back. GoDaddy is the only competitor that structurally could, and its restore paths end at "Once restored, select Publish to make it live" with zero DNS awareness. Base44 hands DNS debugging to whatsmydns.net.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: Registrar + host + CDN in one account. We are the only party who can treat 'the site my customer sees' as a single revertible object spanning build, edge cache and zone file. This also converts our known Domain Connect gap from a liability into a narrower one: for domains already in the user's DreamHost account, our go-live AND our go-back are both one click, which is strictly better than Replit's Entri-automated setup with no rollback.

leapfrog.idea: A branch that is actually safe: forked data and a quarantined mailbox, with a three-group merge diff
leapfrog.spec: "Try it safely" in the version-history menu forks the project onto a preview subdomain (branch-name.yourproject.remixer.app), copies the database schema plus a sampled subset of rows, and — the part nobody can copy — routes ALL outbound mail from the branch to a quarantine inbox at branch@yourdomain, so testing a contact form, an order confirmation or a password reset never reaches a real customer. A persistent amber strip across the top of the branch canvas reads: "Sandbox — separate data, emails go to branch@yourdomain, not to customers." Merging opens a three-group diff — Code changes · Schema changes · Data changes — each collapsible, with the button reading "Merge to live — 4 code changes, 1 new table, 0 data changes". Branches keep full editing capability, including publish-to-preview.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Sandboxing outbound mail requires being the mail provider, and none of them are. Lovable sends 50,000 authenticated emails/month but its docs are explicit that it "does not provide mailboxes." Base44 is send-only via SendGrid CNAMEs and states "Custom email domains are for sending only", with built-in email restricted to registered app users. Bolt's entire domains documentation set contains no mailbox capability at all. Base44 shipped branches in Aug 2026 and had to cripple them — no publishing, secrets, connectors, workflows, code editor, theme settings or version-history restore, and shared production data — precisely because it cannot isolate the runtime side effects.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost operates its own mail platform, so a per-branch catch-all mailbox is a provisioning call, not a product to buy. This turns the most dangerous class of AI-builder mistake — the agent rewriting a form or notification and silently emailing real customers — into a non-event, and it makes "try it safely" a true statement rather than the marketing claim it is at Base44.

leapfrog.idea: Pre-flight cost on the send button
leapfrog.spec: As the user types, a lightweight classifier renders an estimate directly on the send control: "Send · ~0.5–1 cr". Hovering shows the basis in one line: "Estimated from: 1 page, 2 components. You'll see the real cost after." When the estimate exceeds 3 credits the button expands into a two-part control: "Send · ~3–4 cr" plus a secondary "Plan it first · 1 cr". After the turn completes the message footer shows the actual ("0.6 cr · 41s") so the estimate is publicly accountable and users calibrate trust in it.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: It requires committing to a number in advance and eating the variance, and the market leaders have chosen to disclose only after the fact — Lovable shows cost, duration and a permalink in a post-hoc three-dot menu; GoDaddy publishes no per-action costs at all ("The search results don't specify how many credits each individual action uses"); Bolt's reviewers name the gap directly: "Token usage burns faster than you expect on bigger builds, and it is not always clear what a given action will cost before you run it." Bolt's answer was to publish a thrift manual instead.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: Our abstracted credit model makes this defensible in a way Bolt's raw-token model does not — Bolt's cost scales with project file-system size, so an estimate would be meaningless. With 1,000 credits/mo and a bounded action taxonomy, a ±1 credit range is honest and cheap to compute. It is also the single most direct attack on the emotion that dominates every review of every competitor in this dossier.

leapfrog.idea: Production-grounded error recovery: pull the real access, error and mail logs into the builder chat
leapfrog.spec: When a published site errors, the chat surfaces an unprompted card: "Your live site returned 12 errors in the last hour" with a secondary "Show me" that expands real origin log lines (timestamp, path, status, message) as evidence, and a primary "Fix it — free". For mail specifically: "3 form submissions didn't reach hello@yourdomain" with the delivery reason in plain language ("the message was rejected as spam by the receiving server") and a fix action. The card is generated from telemetry, not from the user noticing.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: None of them run the origin. Bolt sends users to the browser console ("CMD + Option + J") and admits its own analytics count bots with no filtering. GoDaddy's documented remedy for a broken preview is to prompt "Restart dev server." v0 hands off to the Vercel dashboard via "Inspect on Vercel." Lovable's Project Monitoring (Beta, Pro+) is the closest analogue but it is a scheduled agent job that inspects the project, not a reader of live server logs, and it "detects but never auto-fixes."
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost already operates the web server and the mail platform and already ingests HTTP access/error and postfix/dovecot logs into a queryable pipeline for support. Feeding that into the builder chat means Remixer is the only AI builder that can say what actually happened to a real visitor or a real email, rather than what the agent believes it built. It also converts post-launch — where every competitor in this dossier is thin — into our strongest chapter.

open_questions: Does publishing genuinely consume credits in Remixer today, and what share of monthly credit burn does it represent? If publish-driven consumption is material, making it free needs a compensating change (higher chat-edit pricing, or a lower monthly grant) rather than a straight give-away — but the competitive exposure is real enough that we should model it this quarter.

What checkpoint model do we actually have? The KB article on Undo/Redo appears to describe the legacy section-based Remixer ('undo and redo buttons on the top left of the edit page'), not the 2026 AI builder. Before designing per-message revert we need to know whether the current builder has any versioning at all, what granularity it stores at, and whether restoring publishes.

Can we snapshot the app database alongside each code version cheaply enough to offer 30-day paired rollback free on a $9.99 plan? What is the per-project storage cost at p50 and p95 project size, and does our existing hosting backup infrastructure cover it or does this need new plumbing?

Do we self-heal today — and are those retries billed? We need the fraction of credits spent on the agent correcting its own output before we can price a 'fixing our own mistakes is free' policy. In my measured v0 run that fraction looked like roughly a third of a single build.

Where does the Visual Editor write, and can a subsequent chat turn silently overwrite manual visual edits? This is Lovable's documented failure ('fine-grained design edits can be overwritten by subsequent prompts'). If we have the same architecture, the free-edit lane and the lock mechanism must ship together or the free lane makes the problem worse.

Do we have per-action credit telemetry with tight enough variance to render a pre-flight estimate? What is the actual distribution of credits per chat turn, and what error band would a classifier produce? An estimate that is wrong by 3x is worse than no estimate.

Is the ~408px chat panel resizable, and is the width persisted? Bolt runs 450px with a brand-tinted drag handle; Hostinger persists width, supports drag-to-hide and double-click-to-reset. This is cheap and we appear to be behind.

Can we quarantine outbound mail per branch without polluting the sending reputation of the customer's real domain? The branch-mailbox leapfrog depends on this being operationally safe, not just technically possible.

What is our position on model choice? Lovable published 'The model picker is a dead end' (11 Aug 2026) and hides it; Base44 gates a 7-model picker at $40/mo and shipped its own Base 1 model; Bolt names agents by outcome ('Standard' / 'Max'); Replit exposes Lite/Economy/Power plus Turbo as an explicit cost dial. Do we expose nothing, an outcome-named pair, or a cost dial?

How fast can SmartEdge purge across all 10 PoPs? The 'roll back the launch' promise needs a number we can put in the confirmation copy. If it is minutes rather than seconds, the copy and the expectation change.

Should design directions be shown before the first build given our 2–3 minute generation is the fastest in the field? Lovable's three-direction step exists partly because its build is expensive; ours may be cheap enough that building one and offering a free 'show me three other directions' afterwards converts better than a pre-build gate. Worth an A/B.

Do we surface a diff of any kind today? Base44 hides diffs behind a per-message hover menu → 'View Changes' precisely so the non-technical default stays clean. If we have no diff surface at all, the cheapest version is a changed-pages summary in the publish dialog, which is an open, upvoted request on Base44's own feedback board.

lens: Publish, domains, hosting, SSL & email — the go-live moment end to end
executive_take:
The brief's stated structural advantage is half gone. Between April and June 2026 this category became registrars. Lovable sells domains in-app, handles transfer-in with EPP codes, toggles WHOIS privacy and auto-writes A/TXT ("Lovable becomes the registrar for that domain"). Vercel sells domains inside v0's publish flow (Publish → Customize → "Buy a Domain") at registrar cost, recently cut up to 50%. Bolt resells with a 60-day transfer lock (Name.com upstream). Base44 resells through Wix or IONOS with DNS+SSL automatic. Emergent — a pure AI startup — resells IONOS free for year one, SSL in under ten minutes. Replit goes from domain search to live "in less than a minute." Selling a domain in-flow is table stakes now, not a moat.

Two things are not. First, one-click external DNS. Lovable and Replit both bought Entri: provider detection, whitelabeled sign-in, records written on the user's behalf, 70+ providers supported; Webflow reports a 2x domain-connect rate and 30% faster conversion after adopting it, and one Entri customer went from 20% to 80% successful connections. Bolt, Base44, Figma and GoDaddy-for-external-domains are all still manual copy-paste plus a "Verify" button and a 24–72 hour shrug. Our verified Domain Connect gap is category-standard today but closing around us, and the fix is a purchase order ($249/mo for 600 domains/yr, $749/mo with custom-domain SSL) rather than a roadmap.

Second, mailboxes. Nobody in the pure-AI set has one. Lovable sends DKIM/SPF/DMARC-authenticated mail from your domain and states plainly it provides no mailboxes. Base44's docs say "Custom email domains are for sending only." Bolt's entire domains doc set never mentions MX for the user. v0 has no email at any tier. Only Hostinger (1/2/5 mailboxes by plan) and GoDaddy (Microsoft 365 resold at $7.99/mo) compete, and both meter it. DreamHost runs its own mail platform at roughly $1.67–1.99/mailbox with 25GB.

So the gap is not "can we sell a domain" — it is the sixty seconds around publish. And we have one self-inflicted wound there: Remixer charges credits to publish. Lovable states publishing is free on every plan and consumes no credits. GoDaddy publishes an explicit no-credit action list. Bolt exempts restores, UI actions and security audits. Base44 exempts all manual visual edits. Metering the moment of success is the single most attackable thing on this lens, and it also suppresses republishing — which produces stale live sites, the exact failure the whole staging/live signalling system exists to prevent.

comparison.approach: Full registrar (buy, transfer in/out via EPP, WHOIS privacy toggle) + Entri one-click DNS for external domains, with manual fallback (A → 185.158.133.1 plus `_lovable` TXT). Named domain state machine — Pending / Live / Ready / Removed, plus Verifying, Unable to verify, Stalled, Offline — each with exactly one recovery verb. Branded workspace URLs progress "Provisioning DNS" → "Issuing SSL certificate" → "Active". SSL automatic with a stated 72-hour escalation SLA and Cloudflare-specific triage (errors 1001/1003 → set records to DNS only, grey cloud). Publish sits top-right beside Share; a dot appears when live is stale; a "Published" badge marks the live version in History; the snapshot model is stated in plain words. Publishing is free on every plan and consumes zero credits. Shippable by chat ("Ship it"). Sends SPF/DKIM/DMARC-authenticated mail from your domain, 50,000/mo — but no mailboxes.
comparison.notes: Best in class by a clear margin. The only weaknesses on this lens: non-primary domains 302-redirect (temporary, wrong for SEO), and at zero credits the backend of a LIVE app pauses — a builder-side balance breaking a customer-facing site.

comparison.approach: Automated external-registrar DNS via Entri — "a third-party service that can sign into your registrar and write records on your behalf, bypassing manual entry" (release note 5 Jun 2026). Sells domains in-app across .com/.ai with auto-configuration: "less than a minute from search to going live" (10 Jul 2026). Manual path needs an A record plus a permanent `replit-verify=` TXT that must never be removed or certificate renewal breaks. Deployment types are priced separately from the plan (Static/Autoscale/Scheduled from $1/mo, Reserved VM from $20/mo). Private/password-protected deployments were pushed down to the free Starter tier on 8 May 2026, which also publishes 1 project. Domains, Auth, Database and Secrets consolidated into one pinned Tools pane (31 Jul 2026).
comparison.notes: A non-registrar, non-host closed the DNS gap by buying it. Proof the capability is off-the-shelf. No email product.

comparison.approach: Publish is a menu → "Publish to Production", live in ~30s, then "Publish Changes"; "Inspect on Vercel" is a deliberate escape hatch and "Fix with v0" appears on failed builds. Two domain entry points (Publish → Customize Domain, or Project Menu → Domains); Add offers a free .vercel.app described as "free and instantly available" with automatic HTTPS, or a custom domain bought in-flow via Vercel's own registrar at registrar cost. Free deployments carry a "Built with v0" badge. Sandbox previews on opaque `{24-char}.v0.build` hosts.
comparison.notes: Strong in-flow purchase, ~30s deploys. But external-domain DNS is punted entirely to the Vercel dashboard with no record types, no verification UI and no guidance in v0's own docs. No email at any tier.

comparison.approach: The closest structural analogue to Remixer: the builder lives inside hPanel, and the domain choice happens BEFORE the build ("choose a domain or use a temporary one"). Mailboxes are an explicit per-tier ladder — Free 0, Explorer 1, Starter 2, Hobbyist 5 per website — and a free domain is included from Starter ($13.99/mo) up. Publish shows a loading percentage, plays a completion sound, then offers exactly two actions: "Copy URL" and "Go to Analytics"; republishing surfaces "Publish changes".
comparison.notes: The only competitor already monetising mailboxes through an AI-builder funnel — direct evidence our email lever converts. But the seams are dangerous: their own docs warn changing a project's domain "resets your email plan and deletes all associated email data", and domain redirection isn't in the builder at all (punt to hPanel → Forward Domain).

comparison.approach: Invented and open-sourced Domain Connect (~50 adopters incl. Microsoft, Google, Squarespace), so GoDaddy-nameserver domains get zero-touch DNS: "Airo AI Builder automatically updates your DNS." External domains are manual at the user's provider. Publish is a bare upper-right button — no modal, no diff, no confirmation. Free sites land on a long autogenerated *.godaddysites.com subdomain with no documented rename. One terminal "Active" DNS status against a stated 48-hour expectation, with no intermediate states. Contact-form sender must be an address on the connected custom domain; mailboxes are paid add-ons (pro email $2.99/user/mo, Microsoft 365 $7.99/mo). Hosting/CDN/WAF is rented Cloudflare. Publishing is not on their credit-consuming list. Downgrade takes the site offline but preserves content and restores on re-engagement.
comparison.notes: The world's largest registrar makes you LEAVE the builder to buy a domain — "Go to GoDaddy domains, search... and then purchase it" then five more steps back. The single biggest unclaimed opening in the category, and the Free tier can't publish at all.

comparison.approach: "Link Domain" button inside the Deployments panel: live IONOS availability search, buy without leaving the product, free for the first year, DNS auto-configured, SSL auto-provisioned, whole thing "typically takes less than 10 minutes, most of which is DNS propagation time." Existing domains get an A record with TTL 300, verified in 5–15 minutes.
comparison.notes: A pure AI startup manufactured registrar economics by reselling someone else's — and set the customer price expectation at free-first-year, which DreamHost can meet natively at better margin. Offsetting flaw: an active deployment costs 50 credits/month in ongoing rent (half a $20 plan) and browser previews expire after 30 minutes.

comparison.approach: AI builder funded by hosting+domain subscription rather than metered credits. All four paid plans (Light $17, Core $29, Business $39, Business Elite $159, annual) include a free custom domain for year one, renewing at roughly $17.35/yr. Prompt-to-live-URL quoted at 5–7 minutes.
comparison.notes: Hard lock-in on this lens: Wix's own docs confirm Harmony sites cannot be exported and support no custom code — if the go-live requirements change, the only path is rebuilding elsewhere. Email is sold separately, not bundled like Hostinger.

comparison.approach: Best-consolidated publish surface in the field: one modal titled "Publish your project" holding visibility (with consequence copy — "Anyone on the web can view it and search engines can find and list it"), Manage access, a free "Run security audit" that settles into "Security audit up to date", an Edit-domain pencil, Publish/Update, and Unpublish (two clicks). Publishing is explicitly not continuous — "changes you make to your Bolt project aren't automatically applied to your published site", you must click "Update". Bought hosting back from Netlify (now opt-in). Sells domains but custom domains are 100% manual DNS — www CNAME and root ALIAS/ANAME/flattened CNAME to `site-dns.bolt.host`, TXT for subdomains, "up to 24 hours", manual "Verify domain status" button — with no Domain Connect even for domains bought through Bolt.
comparison.notes: Zero mailbox capability anywhere in the domains doc set; MX appears only as a record you may add manually for someone else's mail host. Free sites go OFFLINE on bandwidth overage (10GB / 333,333 requests) until the next billing cycle, and free-tier sites are structurally invisible to search because SEO Boost requires a paid plan AND a custom domain.

comparison.approach: Publish menu (copy URL, "Connect a custom domain"/"Get Domain", Share, App Visibility, Publish App) plus the field's best staging primitive: a "Testing Link" where "People who open the testing link see your unpublished changes and interact with test data only" and "the link does not change your live app or production records." Free apps on myapp.base44.app, renamed via Dashboard → Domains → "Edit URL". Buying via Wix or IONOS gets automatic DNS+SSL; external domains are manual — ANAME/ALIAS → base44.onrender.com or A → 216.24.57.1, remove AAAA, fix CAA, no wildcards, 48–72h, then "Verify".
comparison.notes: No way to see what will change before publishing — "Provide an option to preview changes before publishing" is an open, upvoted item on Base44's own feedback board. Docs send DNS debugging to whatsmydns.net. Email is sending-only via SendGrid CNAMEs and built-in email can only reach registered app users — no external addresses, no attachments, no mailboxes.

comparison.approach: Publishing a Framer-subdomain site with SSL is free on the free plan; a custom domain requires Basic ($10/mo) or higher, with a free custom domain promotion on yearly upgrades.
comparison.notes: Clean free-tier publish story, permanent "Made in Framer" badge on free, and a hard 1GB bandwidth ceiling. No registrar, no email, no documented DNS automation.

comparison.approach: Free branded subdomains at `yourapp.ai.studio` (10 Jul 2026), first-come-first-served, chosen before deploy; building, publishing and the shareable link cost nothing, and new users get their first two Google Cloud deploys with no credit card. API keys injected server-side, never in client code.
comparison.notes: Positions the free subdomain as the permanent public address rather than staging — a different framing from Remixer's *.remixer.app. No custom-domain flow documented, no email, and Google killed the predecessor (Firebase Studio, 19 Mar 2026), which is its own trust cost.

comparison.approach: Publish modal in the upper-right containing Title (explained as how it appears "in browser tabs, search engine results, and social media"), URL (auto-generated as three-random-words.figma.site), Status ("Not published"/"Published"), "Who can view" on Org/Enterprise — and a Typography alert flagging missing WOFF/WOFF2 web fonts before you go live. Primary becomes "Update" after first publish; Unpublish lives in "Make settings". Published sites are NOT indexed by search engines by default.
comparison.notes: Weakest domain flow in the sweep: copy a TXT and a CNAME into your registrar by hand, come back and press "Refresh", wait ~15 minutes, error icon if unverifiable. Professional caps at 10 custom domains shared across Make and Sites. No email. The publish-modal font warning is nonetheless the single best pre-flight check anyone ships.

comparison.approach: Editable *.remixer.app staging subdomain with a pencil affordance in the toolbar; centered domain switcher in the top chrome (no competitor puts the live address in primary chrome — a genuine IA advantage); blue Publish top-right; hosting + first-party global CDN (SmartEdge, 10 PoPs) + SSL + domain connection included in the $9.99 plan; 30-day no-card trial where building AND staging publishing are free — the longest no-card trial in the category and better than GoDaddy Free (cannot publish at all) or Base44 Free (5 credits/day). Registrar + host + email provider underneath.
comparison.notes: Held back by four things, all fixable: publishing changes consumes credits (uniquely bad — Lovable, GoDaddy and Bolt all exempt the equivalent); no Domain Connect, so external domains are guided-manual; no documented domain state machine, unpublished-changes signal, publish pre-flight, rollback-to-published-version, or multi-domain/primary/redirect story; and the mailbox capability exists at DreamHost but is not wired into the publish flow at all — the one thing no rival can copy is the one thing we haven't shipped.

best_in_class.why: It is the only product in the field that treats go-live as a designed state machine rather than a button. Three things put it ahead. (1) Staleness is expressed three times without contradiction — a dot on the Publish button when live is older than the current build, a "Published" badge on the live entry in version history, and the snapshot model stated in plain words ("Publishing creates a snapshot of your project. Changes made afterward don't affect the live site until you republish"). Staging-vs-live confusion is the top support cost in site builders and Lovable simply removed the ambiguity. (2) Every domain failure state has a name AND a recovery verb — Verifying → "Check status"; Unable to verify → "DNS verification did not complete within one hour"; Stalled → "Retry"; Offline → "Recover. Review displayed DNS records"; Removed → "Reconnect" — plus progressive provisioning copy ("Provisioning DNS" → "Issuing SSL certificate" → "Active"), a 72-hour SSL escalation SLA, and vendor-specific rescue guidance naming the actual third-party misconfiguration (Cloudflare 1001/1003: set records to DNS only, grey cloud, not Proxied). No dead end lacks a button. (3) Publishing and republishing are free on every plan and consume zero credits, with no visitor, request or bandwidth caps — so the meter never sits between the user and the thing they came for. Add full registrar behaviour (in-app purchase, EPP transfer both directions, WHOIS privacy toggle, domains scoped to the workspace not the project) and Entri one-click DNS for external domains, and Lovable currently beats DreamHost on the journey DreamHost should own outright. Its only real gaps on this lens are 302 rather than 301 redirects for non-primary domains, and — decisively — no mailboxes.

adopt.pattern: Stop charging credits to publish, and say so at the point of the meter
adopt.spec: Remove credit consumption from publish and republish entirely. In the publish sheet, directly beneath the primary Publish button, one line at 13px in tertiary foreground: "Publishing is free. Credits are only used when Remixer builds or edits." In the credits chip popover in the top toolbar, add a second section headed "Always free" listing six rows with check icons: Publishing and republishing · Hosting, SSL and CDN · Connecting or buying a domain · Restoring a version · Editing text and images directly · Fixing an error Remixer caused. Keep the chip's balance readout where it is — it is better placed than GoDaddy's, which exiles the balance to a separate Manage-my-plan page and is their single loudest UX complaint.
adopt.rationale: We are the only major player metering the moment of success. Lovable: "Publishing itself is free. Only backend activity… consumes Run credits." GoDaddy publishes an explicit no-credit action list (Preview, Code, Edit, Media, History restore) with publishing absent from the billable side. Bolt exempts version restores, UI-button actions and security audits. Base44 exempts all manual visual edits. Beyond the competitive optics, charging per publish actively suppresses republishing, which manufactures the stale-live-site problem that every other pattern here exists to solve.

adopt.pattern: Three consistent signals for one deploy state
adopt.spec: (a) A 6px amber dot on the top-right corner of the blue Publish button whenever the current build is newer than the live snapshot. (b) The centered domain switcher gains a status pill: green "Live" when in sync, amber "Not published yet" when never published, amber "4 changes not published" when stale — clicking the pill opens the publish sheet. (c) The version history list marks whichever version is currently live with a green "Live" chip. Publish sheet body copy, verbatim: "Publishing takes a snapshot of your site. Anything you change after this stays private until you publish again."
adopt.rationale: Lovable expresses the same fact in three places without contradiction (Publish dot, "Published" badge in History, plainly-stated snapshot model) and it is the most-cited coherence win in the dossier. Bolt states the same rule ("changes you make to your Bolt project aren't automatically applied to your published site") but only in docs. Our centered domain switcher is already the best-placed home for a live-status pill in the entire field — no competitor puts the live address in primary chrome — so this is cheap for us and structurally unavailable to them.

adopt.pattern: A named domain state machine where every dead end carries exactly one button
adopt.spec: Render domain status as a pill in the domain switcher dropdown and in Settings → Domains. States and colours: Pending (grey) · Provisioning DNS (blue, animated) · Issuing SSL certificate (blue) · Live (green) · Ready (green outline — DNS is configured but the site isn't published; CTA "Publish") · Needs attention (amber) · Offline (red). Every non-green state gets one button and one sentence: Verifying → "Check status"; Unable to verify → "Retry" with "DNS verification didn't finish within an hour. The records may not have propagated yet."; Stalled → "Retry"; Offline → "Recover" (expands to show the exact records we expect vs what we see); Removed → "Reconnect". Add three vendor-specific triage cards that appear only when detected: Cloudflare proxying → "Set these records to DNS only (grey cloud), not Proxied."; AAAA present on @ → "Remove the AAAA record for @ — it overrides your A record."; conflicting CAA → "Add a CAA record allowing letsencrypt.org, or remove the existing one."
adopt.rationale: Lovable ships exactly this and it is the reason DNS doesn't lose them users. Base44 requires the same AAAA and CAA cleanups but buries them in prose and then sends users to whatsmydns.net to debug. Bolt gives a single "Status" column and a manual "Verify domain status" button against "up to 24 hours". GoDaddy has one terminal "Active" state and no intermediate states at all — which is where users actually panic.

adopt.pattern: In-flow domain: a three-way fork with a zero-DNS default
adopt.spec: Publish sheet → "Use a custom domain" opens one surface with three tabs. Tab 1, default when the account has any: "In your DreamHost account" — a searchable list of the user's domains, each row showing the domain, its current use ("not pointed anywhere" / "currently: WordPress"), a green "0 records to change" chip, and a "Connect" button that completes in place without leaving the builder. Tab 2: "Buy a new one" — inline availability search showing first-year price and renewal price side by side in the same row, a single "Register & connect" button, and WHOIS privacy pre-checked with the label "Hide my contact details in WHOIS (free)". Tab 3: "Connect one I own elsewhere" — the one-click flow first, manual records as a disclosure. Never navigate the user out of the builder shell at any point.
adopt.rationale: GoDaddy — the world's largest registrar — fails this: their documented buy path is "Go to GoDaddy domains, search for a desired domain, and then purchase it" then return to the apps page and click through five more steps. Replit does search-to-live "in less than a minute"; Emergent buys through IONOS without leaving the Deployments panel; Bolt shows the renewal cost during checkout. Showing renewal price next to first-year price pre-empts the renewal-cliff resentment that dominates GoDaddy's review corpus.

adopt.pattern: One-click DNS for external domains, with manual as a disclosed fallback rather than the default
adopt.spec: Tab 3 flow: user types their domain → we detect their DNS provider → "We can set this up for you at Namecheap. You'll sign in to Namecheap — Remixer never sees your password." → primary button "Set it up automatically". Beneath it, a collapsed link: "Prefer to do it yourself? Show the records" — revealing a table with a per-row copy button and a host-name hint under the Host column: "@, blank, or your full domain — depends on your provider." On success, fire the state machine into "Provisioning DNS" → "Issuing SSL certificate" → "Live". Buy this rather than build it: Entri covers 70+ DNS providers at $249/mo for 600 automatic connections a year, or $749/mo with custom-domain SSL included.
adopt.rationale: Our Domain Connect gap is currently category-standard — Bolt, Base44, Figma and GoDaddy-for-external all make users copy records by hand — but it is closing around us. Lovable and Replit both integrated Entri; Replit's release note for 5 Jun 2026 reads "custom domain DNS setup automated; users no longer need manual record configuration." Entri's own case data: Webflow reports a 2x domain-connect rate and 30% faster conversion, and one customer moved from 20% to 80% successful connections. The host-name hint copy is lifted from Lovable, who learned it the hard way.

adopt.pattern: A preview link that shares unpublished changes
adopt.spec: In the publish sheet, above the primary action, a secondary row: label "Share a preview", helper text "Send the current unpublished version to someone for review. Your live site won't change.", button "Copy preview link". The link is a signed URL under *.remixer.app, view-only, expiring in 7 days, and renders a slim non-dismissable top banner reading "Preview — this is not the live site." Show the expiry in the sheet: "Link expires in 7 days."
adopt.rationale: Base44's Testing Link is the strongest staging primitive found: "People who open the testing link see your unpublished changes and interact with test data only" and "the link does not change your live app or production records." Lovable ships 7-day view-only preview links that "do not see the Lovable editor, chat, or source code." This is how a non-technical user gets sign-off from a client or a spouse without understanding environments — and it is exactly the moment before a paid custom-domain publish.

adopt.pattern: Restore never auto-publishes, and says what it did not restore
adopt.spec: Any version restore lands in staging only. Confirmation copy on completion: "Restored. Your live site hasn't changed — select Publish to make this version live." The version list keeps the green "Live" chip on the previously published version so the user can see the editing head move while the live marker stays put. Where a database exists, add an amber inline note in the restore dialog before confirming: "Restoring your site does not restore your data. Records added since 4 Aug will stay."
adopt.rationale: GoDaddy gets this exactly right — both the History restore and the Backups restore end with the identical instruction "Once restored, select Publish to make it live", and versions can be previewed before restoring. Meanwhile Lovable ("does not restore or roll back your database data"), Bolt ("Restoring to an earlier project version will not change your current Bolt or Supabase databases") and Base44 all carry the data caveat in docs where nobody reads it. Put it in the dialog.

adopt.pattern: Publish sheet as one surface, with a free pre-flight check
adopt.spec: A single sheet titled "Publish" containing, top to bottom: the live URL row (pencil to edit the *.remixer.app subdomain, or "Use a custom domain" link); a visibility row written as consequences not settings — "Public — anyone on the web can view it, and search engines can list it" / "Private — only people you invite can open it"; a pre-flight checklist that runs free and reports with a four-level icon language (green check = passing, blue lightbulb = suggestion, amber triangle = should fix, red X = will break) across five rows: SSL certificate, web fonts available in production, broken internal links, search-engine indexing, and www/apex pair configured; then the primary Publish button; then "Unpublish" as a quiet text link requiring a second click. Resting state of the checklist after a clean run: "Checks up to date."
adopt.rationale: Bolt consolidates go-live, who-can-see-it, is-it-safe and what's-the-URL into one modal and places its free security audit at the exact moment anxiety peaks — then settles into "Security audit up to date". Figma Make's publish modal carries a Typography alert for missing WOFF/WOFF2 fonts, catching the one thing that reliably renders wrong in production while it can still be fixed. Lovable's four-level icon language (green check / blue lightbulb / amber triangle / red X) is the clearest severity vocabulary in the field. Bolt's visibility copy explains the consequence rather than naming the setting.

adopt.pattern: Multi-domain, one primary, and 301 by default
adopt.spec: Settings → Domains lists every attached domain. Exactly one row carries a "Primary" badge with a "Make primary" action on the others. Every non-primary row shows "→ redirects to example.com" with a select defaulting to "Permanent (301)" and offering "Temporary (302)". Add a companion prompt whenever only half a pair exists: "You've connected www.example.com. Add example.com too?" with a one-click "Add and redirect" button.
adopt.rationale: Lovable supports one primary and 302-redirects the rest — temporary redirects don't pass link equity, so their users silently lose SEO. Base44 doesn't support wildcard subdomains at all.
