Hostinger has no redirection in the builder whatsoever and pushes users into hPanel → Domains → "Forward Domain" to choose HTTP/HTTPS and 302 vs permanent. The whole area is unclaimed, and half-configured www/apex pairs are the most common small-business launch defect.

adopt.pattern: Give the post-publish moment two actions and a sound
adopt.spec: On successful publish the sheet collapses to a success state: the live URL rendered as a copyable chip, and exactly two buttons — "Visit site" (primary) and "View analytics" (secondary). Play a single short completion chime, gated behind a user preference and suppressed under prefers-reduced-motion. On republish, the same state reads "Updated" with the same two actions.
adopt.rationale: Hostinger shows a loading percentage during publish, plays a completion sound when the site goes live, and offers exactly "Copy URL" and "Go to Analytics" — routing users to measurement at the single moment they care most, rather than hoping they find a dashboard later. GoDaddy by contrast has a bare Publish button with no modal, no confirmation and no next action, which wastes the highest-emotion moment in the entire product.

avoid.pattern: Charging credits at the moment of publish
avoid.why: Every serious competitor exempts the go-live action. Lovable: "Publishing itself is free. Only backend activity — such as database operations and AI features — consumes Run credits. A live site with no backend activity incurs no credit charges," with no visitor, request or bandwidth caps. GoDaddy publishes a no-credit action list covering Preview, Code, Edit, Media and History restore, with publishing absent from anything billable. Bolt exempts version restores, UI-button actions and security audits. Base44 exempts every manual visual edit. Metering success is both the most attackable line in a competitive comparison and a direct cause of stale live sites, because users ration republishing.

avoid.pattern: A free or trial tier that can build but cannot publish
avoid.why: GoDaddy's Free plan gives unlimited app creation and 50 AI credits but "can only build, not publish" — it stalls the exact moment that converts, and reviewers measure the free allowance at roughly six prompts (314 credits across 39 prompts on a real build). Our 30-day no-card trial with free staging publishing is materially better; the risk is regressing toward GoDaddy's model to protect margin. The correct paywall is the custom domain, which we already do.

avoid.pattern: A bare Publish button with no pre-flight and no summary of what will change
avoid.why: GoDaddy's documented flow is "in the upper-right, select Publish" — no modal, no plan picker, no confirmation, no changed-files summary. Base44 is worse: "Provide an option to preview changes before publishing" is an open, upvoted item on Base44's own public feedback board, alongside two more requests about restoring the last published version. Users about to make something public want to know what is about to become public.

avoid.pattern: Manual DNS with a manual Verify button and a 24–72 hour shrug
avoid.why: Bolt: root ALIAS/ANAME/flattened CNAME to site-dns.bolt.host plus a TXT for subdomains, "Most domains connect within a few hours, but in some cases, it can take up to 24 hours," verified by pressing "Verify domain status" — and this manual path is not bypassed even for domains bought through Bolt. Base44: 48–72 hours, remove AAAA, fix CAA, no wildcards, then "Verify" — with the docs sending users to whatsmydns.net, i.e. handing DNS debugging to a third-party website. Figma: paste TXT and CNAME, press "Refresh", error icon if unverifiable.

avoid.pattern: 302 as the default redirect for non-primary domains
avoid.why: Lovable's docs state that only one domain can be primary and others 302-redirect — notably temporary, not 301. A temporary redirect does not consolidate link equity, so users who connect both apex and www silently split their SEO. This is a one-character defect with a permanent cost, and it is sitting in the best-in-class product.

avoid.pattern: Selling the domain and then abandoning the user on email
avoid.why: Bolt's complete domains documentation set (domains, connect, purchase, aliases, dns-records, ssl-https, troubleshoot-domain) never mentions mailboxes or MX provisioning for the user — MX appears only as a record type you may add manually for someone else's mail host. Base44 states flatly "Custom email domains are for sending only" and its built-in email "is limited to people who are registered users of your app" with no external addresses and no attachments. Lovable sends authenticated mail from your domain but its docs are explicit that it does not provide mailboxes. v0 has no email product at any tier. The user buys a domain at checkout and then has to go buy Google Workspace.

avoid.pattern: Making the user leave the builder to buy a domain
avoid.why: GoDaddy's own help article for the in-builder path reads: "Go to GoDaddy domains, search for a desired domain, and then purchase it," then return to the Airo apps page, select the app, select Domain, select Settings, Connect Domain, Yes Continue. The largest registrar on earth breaks its own funnel with a context switch at the highest-intent moment in the product.

avoid.pattern: Letting a domain change destroy the user's email
avoid.why: Hostinger's own domain-management doc warns that changing the domain on a Horizons project "resets your email plan and deletes all associated email data" and advises backing up first. This is the specific failure mode a bundled registrar+host+email stack creates if the surfaces aren't transactionally joined — and it is the exact risk Remixer inherits by having the same three capabilities.

avoid.pattern: Letting a builder-side balance take a published customer site offline
avoid.why: Bolt free tier: "Up to 10 GB bandwidth" and 333,333 requests/month, after which the site goes offline until the next billing cycle. Lovable at zero credits: building halts, deployed-app AI features fail and "built-in backend services will pause" — database, storage and auth remain safe but inaccessible, with only static pages still serving. Base44's integration credits are a shared workspace pool consumed by end users, so exhaustion pauses features in the live production app. A live site breaking because the owner ran out of build credits is the most damaging possible failure in this category.

avoid.pattern: Gating basic search visibility behind a paid plan plus a custom domain
avoid.why: Bolt's SEO Boost prerenders pages for crawlers because its output is a client-rendered SPA crawlers cannot execute — but it requires both a paid plan AND a custom domain, and is explicitly unavailable on the free *.bolt.host address. Free-tier sites are therefore structurally invisible to search. A self-inflicted problem resold as a paid feature.

avoid.pattern: Destructive, non-refunding undo as the recovery model
avoid.why: Hostinger: Undo means "your last message and the Horizon's corresponding response are permanently deleted"; Restore confirms "All your messages after this message will be permanently deleted"; and "Undoing or restoring a version does not cost additional credits and does not reinstate credits spent on the reverted messages." GoDaddy is worse on deletion — 30-day support-only retention, by phone, with "Recovery is not guaranteed" and "There is no undo button for deletion."

avoid.pattern: Shipping analytics that count bots, and admitting it
avoid.why: Bolt's own docs concede the analytics product includes "visits and actions from web crawlers and bots" with no built-in filtering, so "reported page views, sessions, and other engagement metrics may be higher than actual human activity." Honest, but it makes the paid feature useless for any decision — and post-launch measurement is the one surface where a real host should be unbeatable.

leapfrog.idea: Zero-record go-live: "Your domain is already here."
leapfrog.spec: At first publish, query the signed-in DreamHost account for domains the user already owns that aren't serving a site. Surface the best candidate as the default option at the top of the publish sheet, above the staging URL: a single row reading "example.com is in your DreamHost account" with a green chip "0 records to change" and one button, "Connect and publish". On click: write the records server-side, provision the certificate, and resolve to Live — target under 60 seconds, with the state machine visibly stepping through "Provisioning DNS" → "Issuing SSL certificate" → "Live". Never show a record table, never ask the user to open another tab, never mention nameservers. If the domain currently serves something else, show "currently: WordPress" and require one confirmation: "Replace what's at example.com with this site?"
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Lovable, Vercel, Bolt, Base44, Emergent and Replit are all registrars or resellers now, but they can only automate the domain they sell you TODAY. None of them is the registrar of the domain you bought three years ago and never used — for that they fall back to Entri or to a copy-paste record table. GoDaddy is the one company that structurally could do this and instead ejects the user to the storefront and back through six steps. It requires being the incumbent registrar and DNS operator for a domain that predates the builder, which is a position you cannot buy.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost already holds a large book of registered domains with no live site attached. That is a targetable list, not a funnel — and it converts the single most abandoned step in the category (custom domain attach) into one button with nothing to configure. It also reframes the trial: instead of "publishing to a custom domain is paid", the pitch becomes "the domain you're already paying us for goes live in a minute".

leapfrog.idea: A real mailbox in the publish flow — "Publish gets you a website. It should also get you an address."
leapfrog.spec: Immediately after a custom domain goes Live, the publish success state offers one additional card: heading "Get hello@example.com", a single prefilled text field (`hello`) with the domain appended as static text, a "Create mailbox" button, and helper copy "25GB, webmail, spam filtering. Included with your plan. We'll set the MX records for you." On click, provision the mailbox and write MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC in the same transaction that already wrote the A record — so alignment is correct by construction rather than by user effort. Show the result as a row in Settings → Domains: "hello@example.com — Live · Open webmail". Bundle exactly one mailbox per published custom domain in the $9.99 Remixer Build plan; sell additional mailboxes as an upsell.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: You have to own a mail platform. Lovable built its own outbound delivery infrastructure with auto-managed SPF/DKIM/DMARC and 50,000 messages a month included — and still states plainly it does not provide mailboxes, because inbound mail is a different, much heavier business. Base44's docs say "Custom email domains are for sending only" and route through SendGrid CNAMEs. Bolt's domain docs never mention MX for the user. v0 has no email at any tier. The only two competitors who offer mailboxes both resell or meter them: Hostinger ladders 1/2/5 mailboxes across $6.99/$13.99/$39.99 tiers, and GoDaddy resells Microsoft 365 at $7.99/mo.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost operates its own mail platform at roughly $1.67–1.99 per mailbox per month with 25GB, webmail and spam filtering, and already ships a 3-month Professional Email trial with hosting plans. Bundling one mailbox into a $9.99 plan costs us cents and is literally unmatchable by Lovable, Bolt, v0 or Base44 at any price. It also changes the plan's story from "AI credits" to "your business online" — which is a defensible position when the credit race bottoms out.

leapfrog.idea: A contact form that actually works on day one, because we own the whole mail path
leapfrog.spec: When Remixer generates a contact form, wire it to the mailbox created above with no configuration screen: From `noreply@theirdomain`, Reply-To the visitor, To the owner's new mailbox — with SPF, DKIM and DMARC already aligned because we control the zone. Surface it as a green row in the publish pre-flight checklist: "Contact form → hello@example.com · verified, sending from your domain." If the user later changes the To address, validate it inline; if they point it at a Gmail address, show "We'll send from noreply@example.com so it passes spam checks" rather than silently degrading.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Base44's built-in email "is limited to people who are registered users of your app" and supports neither external addresses nor attachments — so a contact form emailing the owner's own inbox is not a first-class path on the platform. GoDaddy configures the sender address by instructing users to paste GoDaddy-authored prompt strings into the AI chat ("Change my To email address to [your GoDaddy Conversations email here]") — prompt-as-config, non-discoverable, and it spends metered credits to change a setting. Lovable can send authenticated mail but has no inbox to deliver it to.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: Registrar + DNS operator + mail host means the From domain, the DKIM key, the MX record and the destination inbox are all ours in a single transaction. Nobody else can make deliverability correct-by-construction; they can only document what the user should go and configure. This turns the most commonly broken small-business feature into a zero-config one.

leapfrog.idea: Post-launch infrastructure telemetry — warn before the site breaks, not after
leapfrog.spec: Add a "Site health" panel to the right icon rail, showing four persistent rows only a registrar+host+DNS operator can compute. (1) Domain expiry: "example.com renews in 41 days · Auto-renew on" with one-click renew and an amber state under 30 days. (2) Certificate: "SSL valid until 12 Nov · renews automatically". (3) DNS drift: "Your A record changed outside Remixer on 9 Aug — example.com now points to 203.0.113.4" with a "Restore the record" button. (4) Mail health: "SPF, DKIM and DMARC aligned" or an amber "DMARC missing — some mail may be filtered · Fix". Use the four-level icon language from the publish pre-flight so the vocabulary is shared. Notify by email on any row entering amber or red.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Lovable, Bolt, v0 and Base44 only know about a domain while it resolves to them — Lovable's "Offline" state is detected after the site is already down, and its Project Monitoring (Beta, Pro+) audits the code, not the infrastructure. None of them holds the authoritative zone or the WHOIS record, so none can see an expiry approaching, a record edited at another provider, or a DMARC policy drifting. GoDaddy holds the registrar data but rents its edge from Cloudflare and never surfaces any of it in the Airo builder.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: We are the registrar (expiry, auto-renew state), the DNS operator (drift detection against our own zone), the mail host (alignment and blocklist status) and the CDN (SmartEdge, 10 first-party PoPs — so we can honestly measure TTFB per PoP rather than reporting bot-inflated numbers like Bolt does). This converts hosting, normally invisible commodity plumbing, into a visible reason the $9.99 subscription keeps being worth paying after launch — which is the retention problem every credit-metered builder has and none of them can solve.

open_questions: What is the actual credit cost of a publish today, and what share of monthly credit consumption does publishing represent? We need that number to size the revenue impact of making publish free — which is the single highest-leverage change on this lens.

Buy or build one-click external DNS? Entri is $249/mo for 600 automatic connections a year, $749/mo with custom-domain SSL, covering 70+ providers — and Lovable and Replit both bought it. Implementing the Domain Connect spec ourselves (GoDaddy open-sourced it; ~50 providers support it) is cheaper long-term but slower and narrower. Which wins depends on the next question.

What is our actual split at publish time between (a) domains already in the user's DreamHost account, (b) domains they want to buy from us now, and (c) domains held at an external registrar? If (a) dominates, the zero-record go-live flow is the whole game and external DNS automation is a long tail. If (c) dominates, Entri is urgent.

Can the existing DreamHost mail API provision a mailbox and write MX/SPF/DKIM/DMARC transactionally alongside the A record at publish time, and what is the abuse exposure of auto-provisioning mailboxes on a low-friction 30-day no-card trial? Does the mailbox need to be gated behind first payment?

Do we currently support multiple domains, a designated primary and redirects at all — and if so, do we emit 301 or 302? Lovable's 302 default is a live SEO defect in the category leader and we should not copy it.

What happens to a published Remixer site when credits hit zero or the subscription lapses? Lovable pauses backend services on a live app; Bolt takes free sites offline on bandwidth overage; GoDaddy takes the site offline but preserves content and restores it on re-engagement. Our policy needs to be decided and written down before someone discovers it the hard way.

Is there any rollback to a previously published version today, and does restoring auto-publish? GoDaddy's decoupling (restore lands in staging, publish is a separate act) is the right model and we should confirm we match it.

What are our real SSL issuance p50/p95 and DNS propagation-to-live times? Lovable is the only player in the field making a stated commitment ("if not issued after 72 hours, users should contact support"). If our numbers are good, publishing a number is free trust.

Do we offer DNSSEC and WHOIS privacy on Remixer-purchased domains, and should privacy be free and pre-checked? Lovable auto-enables WHOIS privacy; GoDaddy charges extra for Private Registration on top of its free-domain voucher. Free-and-default is a cheap differentiator.

Should the staging *.remixer.app subdomain be positioned as temporary staging or, like Google's yourapp.ai.studio, as a legitimate permanent free address? That choice determines whether the custom domain is the paywall or merely an upgrade — and it changes the trial's conversion story.

Can we measure and surface per-PoP TTFB from SmartEdge honestly in a post-launch panel? Bolt ships analytics that admit to counting bots; if our first-party edge lets us report real human traffic and real latency, that is a durable advantage over every competitor renting Cloudflare, Render or Vercel.

lens: Monetisation UX: pricing, credits, paywalls, upgrade moments
executive_take:
The category has converged on one rule Remixer breaks: never charge for the act of shipping. Lovable states it outright — "Publishing itself is free. Only backend activity... consumes Run credits." GoDaddy's rule is "Credits are used when you perform an action that uses Airo AI Builder's agents... Credits are not used for non-agent actions," and publishing is a non-agent action. Bolt, Base44, v0, Hostinger, Figma Make and Replit all meter generation only. Across fourteen products the sole analogue is Emergent, which charges 50 credits/month as rent on an active deployment and sits near 2.7/5 on Trustpilot. Remixer charging credits to publish a change appears to be unique in the field, and it is the worst available placement: it taxes the moment of success, it double-charges when the agent's own error must be fixed and then re-shipped, and it contradicts our own structural story that we are the host.

The real state of the art is not the price — it is the published free-action list. Lovable exempts publishing, hosting/SSL/CDN, security scans, "Try to fix", the first 100 inline text edits per user per day, and comments. Base44 exempts manual visual edits and all database reads/writes. Replit's Element Editor writes text, size, weight, alignment, colour, margin and padding straight to source for zero credits. GoDaddy's docs actively steer users away from the meter: "use Edit instead of typing a prompt. It's free." Figma Make goes furthest — direct manipulations stage in the prompt box, credit-free, until you apply. Every one of these removes a specific charge that generates rage while leaving the meter running on real work.

The second consensus is cheap thinking, expensive doing: Lovable Plan at a flat 1.00 credit, Base44 Discuss at a flat 0.3. Remixer has neither.

The genuine competitive gap is forecasting. Nobody shows cost before you spend. Lovable reveals it after the fact in a three-dot menu; Bolt's own reviewers name the absence. Combine free publishing, a free-action list and a pre-flight estimate with a spend cap, and Remixer moves from worst-placed paywall in the field to the only builder you can trust with a credit card.

comparison.approach: Unified credit pool (Build + Cloud + AI Gateway) at $25/100 credits, no seats. Publishing, hosting, SSL, CDN, both security scans, "Try to fix", design-system verification and the first 100 inline text edits per user per day are all explicitly free. Plan mode is a flat 1.00 credit vs 0.50–2.00 variable Build. Per-message cost visible in a three-dot menu. 5 free daily credits on every tier including Free. Staged low-credit UX: soft nudge above the chat input, then a blocking dialog at zero, plus a "credits ping" to workspace owners. Top-ups $0.30/credit Pro, auto top-up at 25/50/100.
comparison.notes: Best free-action policy in the field and the only one that systematically refuses to charge for its own mistakes. Undermined by expiry: monthly credits die 2 months after issue, annual 1 month after period end, and the pricing FAQ carries three defensive questions ('Do credits expire?', 'What happens to my credits if my subscription ends?', 'Are credits refundable?'). Trustpilot: "The subscription is basically extortion." At zero credits backend services pause, so a live customer-facing app can break because the owner ran out of BUILD credits. Business costs 2x Pro for identical 100 credits.

comparison.approach: Raw LLM token metering, not abstracted credits. Bolt's own FAQ concedes the driver: "Most token usage is related to syncing your project's file system to the AI: the larger the project, the more tokens used per message." Public Pro is $25 'Start at 10M tokens'; the real ladder (Pro 50/100/200 at $50–$200) only appears after signup. Free is 300K/day and 1M/month. Publishing, version restores, UI-button actions and security audits cost no tokens. Paid tokens roll over 2 months, FIFO. Subscriptions non-refundable.
comparison.notes: Cost scales with project SIZE rather than user intent, so a button-colour change on a large project can cost more than a whole feature on a small one. No per-message readout and no pre-flight estimate — reviewers: "it is not always clear what a given action will cost before you run it." Error loops bill at full price; reviewers estimate up to half their tokens went to errors. Bolt publishes a token-thrift guide, which is good service and an admission the model is hostile. The 300K free daily cap can expire before the documented ~5-minute first build finishes.

comparison.approach: Two currencies: message credits you burn building (0.5 simple / ~1 small feature / ~2 complex module / 3–4 app-wide; Discuss flat 0.3) and integration credits burned at RUNTIME by your live app's end users (email 1, image 1, video 5/sec, LLM 1–15, in-app agent messages 3–40). $16–$160/mo annual. Manual visual edits and all database reads/writes cost zero credits. No rollover. 'Premium' is a first-class semantic design token with full state coverage.
comparison.notes: The zero-credit manual-edit rule is the single smartest pricing decision in the sweep, and splitting build-time from run-time cost is more honest than one pool. But integration credits are a shared workspace pool consumed by your customers, so a viral app pauses live features — the harshest paywall placement in the category. Free is throttled to 5 credits/DAY, making one evening's session impossible. Docs state flatly: "Credits are non-refundable for tool behavior and AI mistakes." Two first-party sources contradict each other on whether top-ups exist at all.

comparison.approach: One clean rule: "Credits are used when you perform an action that uses Airo AI Builder's agents... Credits are not used for non-agent actions." Published free list covers Preview, Code, non-AI Edit, uploads, Media and History restore; publishing is a non-agent action and is not billed. Free 50 credits/mo but ZERO publishing; Starter $9.99 annual/150 credits/1 published site; Pro $24.99/300/10; Ultimate $99.99/750/50. Agent self-heals its own code errors without consuming credits. Spend order is expiry-first, stated. Out-of-credits message names the exact reset time.
comparison.notes: The clearest billing rule in the field and the paywall is a single legible boundary. But the balance is exiled to a separate Manage-my-plan page — reviewers call it "a nuisance" and it is the loudest UX complaint. 50 free credits buys roughly six prompts at the measured ~8 credits/prompt (314 credits over 39 prompts). Free tier cannot publish at all, so the free user hits a wall rather than a pitch. No per-action credit costs are published anywhere, and the surrounding SKU stack (Airo Plus $59.88 renewing $95.88, All Access renewing $323.88) generates the renewal-cliff resentment GoDaddy is known for.

comparison.approach: Raw input/output token metering converted to credits. Free $0 with $5 credits AND a hard 7-messages/day cap; then a cliff straight to Plus $30/user/mo — there is no individual paid plan since Premium was sunsetted. Rates run v0 Mini $0.20 in/$1.20 out to v0 Max Fast $10/$50 per 1M — a 40x output spread — and v0 Max, the second-dearest tier, is the DEFAULT for a new anonymous user. Credits roll over and expire at 65 days; purchased credits last a year and survive a lapsed subscription. Publishing is not separately metered. Free deployments carry a 'Built with v0' badge.
comparison.notes: Best proof-before-ask funnel anywhere — I confirmed a complete anonymous build with no account — but the billing is the field's least forgivable. Community thread 'Credits are burning way too fast': "I spent 30$ in a single day just to add a couple of category pages... We are literally paying for all the good/bad codes that v0 generates." elliottux measured ~20% of iterations were corrections for functionality v0 itself broke. In my own run roughly a third of visible steps fixed an incompatibility in v0's own starter Button component. The FAQ answers 'Why do v0 agents keep failing and consuming my credits?' with a request for feedback and no refund policy.

comparison.approach: The only vendor publishing a per-action credit price list: full landing page ~300 credits, responsive layout 150, large edit 100, small edit 50, with model multipliers stated (Sonnet 4.6 at 0.9x, Opus 4.8 at 1.8x). External agents via MCP consume zero Framer credits. Free 500 credits/day resetting daily (≈2 landing pages), Basic $10/1,000 per month, Pro $30/3,000, top-ups anytime. Publishing a Framer subdomain site with SSL is free.
comparison.notes: Highest transparency score in the sweep on this lens specifically. Publishing an action-to-price table plus model multipliers converts an opaque meter into something a user can budget against — nobody else does this. Weaknesses are narrower scope and no rollover on the free daily grant, but on pure monetisation legibility Framer is the model to copy for our per-action table.

comparison.approach: Direct manipulation via a right-hand properties panel stages every edit in the prompt box, credit-free, until you hit apply — only then does it burn credits and cut a version. Full-seat allowances: 3,000/mo Professional, 3,500 Org, 4,250 Enterprise; Starter and View seats 500/mo plus a 150/day cap. No rollover. Shared team credit subscriptions from 11 Mar 2026, pay-as-you-go with spend limit from Q2 2026.
comparison.notes: Owns the single best mechanism in the entire field — decoupling visual fiddling from the meter and giving the user a reviewable batch before committing spend. Ruined by execution around it: Full-seat limits were enforced retroactively on 18 Mar 2026 and the forum recorded a user dropping from ~200,000 credits/month to 3,000 (98.5%), a $200+ overage month inside base credits, and a thread arguing extra credits are 5.6x more expensive than adding a seat. Plan mode costs MORE credits than build mode — the inverse of Lovable and Base44, and an anti-pattern.

comparison.approach: Free Starter can publish 1 project, including private/password-protected. Core $20/mo annual with $25 monthly credits, Pro $95 with $100. Element Editor writes text content, font size and weight, alignment, text and background colour, margin and padding directly to source with NO credits, escalating to Agent only when scope exceeds that. Cost/quality exposed as a user-facing dial: Lite / Economy / Power, plus a Turbo toggle for 2.5x speed at higher cost. Deployments billed separately from $1/mo.
comparison.notes: Free direct edits with automatic escalation is the cleanest paid boundary in the field — drawn at 'does this need the model', not 'is this an edit'. And letting the free tier publish is the correct paywall placement. But 'Effort-Based Pricing (pay-as-you-go)' appears as a FAQ topic on the pricing page without being defined there, and the opacity produced real bill shock: The Register (18 Sep 2025) reported a user who normally spends $100–$250/month burning $70 in a single night at Agent 3 launch.

comparison.approach: Credits sold as hosting add-ons, not as the product: Free 5 credits, Explorer $6.99/30, Starter $13.99/70, Hobbyist $39.99/200. Mailboxes ladder per tier (0/1/2/5) and free domain from Starter up. Stated rule: "AI credits are used when you create or edit websites by chatting with AI. Credit usage depends on the complexity of each generation." Undo and restore cost no credits — and refund none.
comparison.notes: The bundling shape is right and is the closest structural mirror of Remixer — mailboxes as a per-tier ladder is exactly the lever we hold. But the credit design is punishing: 30 prompts/month on Explorer, and the code editor is paywalled at $39.99 so cheap-tier users must spend a credit on every CSS tweak, making the cheap tiers structurally more expensive to use. Undo/restore is destructive and explicitly non-refunding: "All your messages after this message will be permanently deleted."

comparison.approach: Free 10 credits; Standard $20/mo (100 credits), Pro $200 (750), Team $300 (1,250). Top-ups $10 per 50 credits, never expire. An ACTIVE DEPLOYMENT costs 50 credits per month on an ongoing basis.
comparison.notes: The only product in this sweep that charges recurring credits for keeping something live — a shipped app consumes half a Standard plan's monthly allowance just by existing. This is the closest analogue to Remixer's publish charge and it maps to the worst reputation in the sweep: Trustpilot around 2.7/5, r/vibecoding reporting credits "burn way too fast", and browser previews expiring after 30 minutes. Read this as the cautionary case for taxing the live state.

comparison.approach: $9.99/mo billed yearly ($119.88) or $9.99 first month then $14.99/mo. 1,000 credits/mo plus 1,000 bonus in month one. Top-ups +1,000 = $14.99, +2,500 = $34.99. 30-day free trial, no credit card — the longest no-card trial in the category. Building is free in trial; publishing to a custom domain is paid. Persistent credits chip in the top toolbar. Credits are consumed by generation, chat edits AND publishing changes.
comparison.notes: Genuinely ahead on three things: cheapest entry price (ties GoDaddy Starter, beaten only by Hostinger's $6.99), the persistent toolbar credits chip (GoDaddy's balance is exiled to a separate page and it is their loudest complaint), and published fixed top-up packs with visible prices (GoDaddy publishes none, v0 has no packs, Base44's own sources contradict each other). Behind on everything else: uniquely charging for publishing, no published free-action list, no plan/discuss mode, no per-message cost receipt, no pre-flight estimate, undocumented expiry and spend order, and a credit unit whose value is unpublished. Top-up maths also carries a 50% premium over the included rate ($0.015 vs $0.00999/credit) and the 2,500 pack is only ~6.7% cheaper per credit than the 1,000 pack — a very weak volume curve.

best_in_class.why: Not because its pricing is cheap or its expiry rules are fair — they are not, and the 'basically extortion' Trustpilot review is earned. Lovable wins this lens because it is the only product that has systematically enumerated the specific charges which generate rage and removed each one individually, while leaving the meter running on genuine work. The list is precise and published: publishing and republishing are free; hosting, SSL and CDN are free; both Basic and Deep security scans cost zero credits; 'Try to fix' on errors and 'Try to fix all' on security findings are 'free within our fair use policy'; design-system verification turns are 'billed at zero credits'; and the first 100 inline text edits per user per day are free, which surgically eliminates the single most infuriating possible charge — being billed to fix a typo. Around that it builds the supporting instrumentation nobody else assembles in one place: Plan mode at a flat 1.00 credit so thinking is cheap and predictable while doing is metered; exact per-message cost behind a three-dot menu at the point of consumption; a two-stage low-credit UX that nudges above the chat input before it blocks at zero; a 'credits ping' that lets a team member ask an owner for more without leaving the flow; 5 free daily credits on every tier including Free, which converts the free plan into a habit loop rather than a countdown; and no seats at all — 'plans are priced by the credits they include, not by seats.' The lesson for Remixer is the shape, not the price. Lovable's failures are equally instructive and equally avoidable: credit expiry at 2 months, forfeiture on cancellation, and the decision that zero credits pauses backend services on a LIVE app so a customer-facing product can break because the owner ran out of build credits. Copy the free-action discipline; refuse the expiry clock and the live-app hostage.

adopt.pattern: Stop charging credits for publishing, and put it in the pricing headline
adopt.spec: Remove credit consumption from publish and republish entirely. The Publish button in the top toolbar never displays a credit cost and never opens a confirm-spend step. Pricing page gains one line directly beneath the $9.99 Build price: 'Publishing is free. Hosting, CDN and SSL are included. Credits only pay for the AI.' Add a three-row comparison strip on the pricing page — 'Publish a change' / 'Keep it live' / 'Fix an AI mistake' — with a green tick in the Remixer column. In the builder, the stale-changes indicator on Publish stays, but carries no price.
adopt.rationale: Across fourteen products only Emergent charges anything for the live state (50 credits/month deployment rent) and it carries the worst reputation in the sweep (~2.7/5 Trustpilot). Lovable is explicit — 'Publishing itself is free... A live site with no backend activity incurs no credit charges.' GoDaddy's rule is 'Credits are used when you perform an action that uses Airo AI Builder's agents... Credits are not used for non-agent actions.' Charging for publish taxes the moment of success, double-charges when the agent's own error must be fixed then re-shipped, suppresses the publish frequency that drives retention and domain attach, and contradicts our structural claim to be the host.

adopt.pattern: An 'Always free' panel inside the credits chip popover
adopt.spec: Clicking the credits chip in the top toolbar opens a 320px popover with three stacked sections. (1) Balance: '812 of 1,000 credits' with a 4px progress bar, and beneath it in 12px secondary text 'Resets 1 Sep'. (2) 'Always free' — a checklist with green ticks: Publishing and republishing · Hosting, SSL and CDN · Visual Editor edits · Restoring a version · Connecting a domain · Fixing Remixer's own errors. (3) 'What costs credits' — a two-column table: New page or section ~40 · Chat edit ~10 · Full site generation ~120 · Plan message 1 (flat). Footer: 'Top up' (secondary) and 'Manage plan' (ghost).
adopt.rationale: Our persistent toolbar chip already beats GoDaddy, whose balance lives on a separate Manage-my-plan page and is described by reviewers as 'a nuisance' and their top complaint. But a balance alone is a threat; a balance plus a free-action list is a boundary. Lovable, GoDaddy, Base44, Bolt and Replit all publish free-action lists in docs — none puts one in the product at the point of anxiety. Framer is the only vendor publishing per-action prices (300 landing page / 150 responsive layout / 100 large edit / 50 small edit); adopting that table in-product makes the meter budgetable.

adopt.pattern: Plan mode as a composer pill, flat-priced and cheaper than building
adopt.spec: A pill toggle in the chat composer immediately left of Send, labelled 'Plan', which fills with the indigo AI gradient when active (matching Bolt's 'highlights blue when active'). First-run tooltip: 'Plan mode talks through changes without touching your site. Flat 1 credit per message.' The plan response terminates in a primary blue button 'Build this plan' which switches the composer back to Build mode automatically. Keyboard: Cmd+. / Ctrl+. toggles, and must work mid-typing without losing the in-flight text.
adopt.rationale: The cheap-thinking/expensive-doing split is now consensus: Lovable Plan is a flat 1.00 credit against 0.50–2.00 variable Build; Base44 Discuss is a flat 0.3 against 0.5–4; Bolt states 'Plan mode uses fewer tokens because it doesn't make any changes to your project.' It converges users on a spec before an expensive build turn, is the cheapest possible undo (nothing was built), and makes the pricing itself an affordance. Base44's Cmd+. working mid-typing is the craft detail — intent changes mid-sentence. Do NOT copy Figma Make, whose plan mode costs MORE than build mode.

adopt.pattern: Free direct manipulation in the Visual Editor, labelled free, with visible escalation
adopt.spec: Every edit made by direct manipulation in the Visual Editor writes to source with no agent call and no credits: text content, font family/size/weight, alignment, text colour, background colour, padding and margin per side, corner radius, opacity. The Visual Editor panel header carries a small green chip reading 'Free'. When the selection needs the agent — structural change, new component, new page — the panel replaces the property controls with an inline escalation row: 'This needs the AI — about 8 credits.' plus an 'Ask Remixer' button that pre-fills the composer with the element reference attached.
adopt.rationale: Replit's Element Editor covers this exact property list credit-free and escalates automatically; Base44 exempts 'manual visual edits (dragging, layout changes, direct text editing)' plus all database reads/writes; Lovable makes the first 100 inline text edits per user per day free; GoDaddy's docs actively steer users off the meter — 'use Edit instead of typing a prompt. It's free, and Airo AI Builder can't make unintended changes when you're editing directly.' The paid boundary should be 'does this need the model', not 'is this an edit'. It also teaches the economically correct habit: AI for structure, hands for polish.

adopt.pattern: Fixing our own mistakes is free, by published policy
adopt.spec: When a generation errors, a build check fails, or a post-change verification detects a regression, the chat shows an error card with a primary button 'Fix this — free' and a subline 'Fixes for Remixer's own errors don't use credits.' Same treatment for security and SEO scans: the scan is free, and 'Fix all' is free. Add the line to the credits popover's Always-free list and to the pricing FAQ.
adopt.rationale: This is the single most effective antidote to credit resentment. Lovable makes 'Try to fix' and 'Try to fix all' free within fair use and both security scans zero-credit; Bolt's security audits cost no tokens; GoDaddy's agent validates and repairs its own code and a reviewer confirmed 'it fixed it without consuming any AI credits.' The inverse is the most inflammatory line in Base44's documentation — 'Credits are non-refundable for tool behavior and AI mistakes' — and third-party analysis frames the whole category problem precisely: 'every bug the AI introduces is a future credit charge for the user to fix, not for the platform to prevent.' Because Remixer also charges to publish, we currently bill twice for one defect.

adopt.pattern: Per-message cost receipt under every AI response
adopt.spec: Beneath each completed AI response, a '···' overflow menu containing, in order: 'Cost: 12 credits · 41s', 'Copy', 'Revert to here'. Hovering the cost line opens a breakdown tooltip: '4 files changed · 1 image generated · 2 pages rebuilt'. The cost line is plain secondary text, not a warning colour — it is a receipt, not an alarm.
adopt.rationale: Lovable is the only builder shipping this: 'click the three-dot menu below any Lovable response in the chat to see its exact cost.' The dossier names it as its main mitigation against credit anxiety. Its absence is a documented weakness elsewhere — Bolt reviewers: 'Token usage burns faster than you expect on bigger builds, and it is not always clear what a given action will cost before you run it.' Surfacing cost at the point of consumption converts an opaque monthly drain into a series of legible, attributable transactions.

adopt.pattern: Two-stage low-credit UX, with the live-site guarantee in the copy
adopt.spec: At 15% remaining, a non-blocking strip appears directly above the chat composer with a 3px amber left border (our amber = action-needed token): '142 credits left this month. Resets 1 Sep.' plus a 'Top up' text button. At zero, a blocking dialog — title 'You're out of credits'; body 'Your site stays live and everything you've published keeps working. You'll get 1,000 more on 1 September, or top up now to keep building.'; buttons 'Top up 1,000 — $14.99' (primary blue) and 'Wait until 1 Sep' (ghost). Teams get a third option: 'Ask an owner for credits'.
adopt.rationale: Lovable stages exactly this — 'a nudge appears above the chat input with your remaining credits and an option to add more', then 'a blocking dialog until credits are available' — and adds a 'credits ping to workspace owners and admins'. GoDaddy names the reset time in its out-of-credits message, converting a dead end into a wait-or-pay choice. The 'your site stays live' clause is our differentiator and must be stated: at zero, Lovable pauses backend services so a live customer-facing app can break, and Base44's end-user-consumed integration credits pause live features mid-month.

adopt.pattern: State the spend order, and make it expiry-first
adopt.spec: One line in the credits popover beneath the balance: 'We spend the credits closest to expiring first — free and bonus credits before ones you paid for.' Repeat verbatim in the pricing FAQ under a question titled 'Which credits get used first?'
adopt.rationale: GoDaddy states it plainly — 'Airo Builder uses credits in order of expiration, starting with those expiring soonest. This includes both free and paid credits' — and Lovable documents the same rule ('always uses usage-specific grants before general credits'). Neither surfaces it prominently in-product. It costs one line and removes the specific low-grade suspicion that the vendor is burning the credits you paid for while your free grant quietly expires. Remixer's 1,000 first-month bonus credits make this urgent: users must be told the bonus is spent first.

adopt.pattern: A daily free grant that survives the trial cliff
adopt.spec: Alongside the 30-day trial, every account — in trial, lapsed, or paid — receives a small daily grant (start at 30 credits/day, resetting 00:00 UTC, no rollover). Shown in the credits popover as its own line above the monthly balance: 'Daily free credits: 30 · resets in 6h 12m'. On day 31 of an unconverted trial the builder does not go dark; it drops to the daily grant with a strip reading 'Your trial ended. You still get 30 free credits a day — enough for small edits. [See plans]'.
adopt.rationale: The field has abandoned timed trials for perpetual free with a habit loop: Lovable gives 5 daily build credits at 00:00 UTC on Free, Pro and Business (the dossier calls it 'a genuine habit loop'); v0 Plus gives '$2 of free daily credits on login per user'; Framer free is 500/day. Our 30-day no-card trial is genuinely the longest in the category, but it is a cliff — on day 31 the tyre-kicker is gone with no return path. A daily grant keeps a lapsed user's site editable and their account warm, which matters far more for a host that also wants the domain renewal.

adopt.pattern: 'Premium' as a first-class semantic token intent
adopt.spec: Add a full token family for monetisation surfaces — fill and border in primary/secondary/light/ghost across default/hover/active/disabled, plus a dedicated focus ring — derived from the existing indigo→purple Remixer AI gradient rather than inventing a gold or amber upsell colour. Every credits chip, top-up button, plan gate, upgrade CTA and locked-feature badge draws exclusively from it. Amber stays reserved for 'action needed'; blue stays reserved for 'action'.
adopt.rationale: Base44 ships exactly this: --sem-fill-premium-{primary,secondary,light,ghost} × {default,hover,active,disabled}, --sem-border-premium-*, --focus-ring-premium and --gradient-premium. The result is that every paywall in the product reads as an intentional part of the interface rather than a nag bolted on. Most products accumulate ad-hoc gold badges that look cheap and inconsistent; systematising monetisation as a designed intent is what makes gates feel like part of the product rather than an interruption of it.

avoid.pattern: Charging any credit for the live state — per-publish or as monthly deployment rent
avoid.why: Emergent is the only product in the sweep that does it (50 credits/month for an active deployment, half a Standard plan's allowance consumed by an app merely existing) and it carries the worst standing in the sweep: Trustpilot around 2.7/5 with r/vibecoding reporting credits 'burn way too fast'. Every credible competitor exempts publishing explicitly — Lovable ('Publishing itself is free'), GoDaddy ('Credits are not used for non-agent actions'), Bolt (UI-button actions and restores cost no tokens), Base44, Hostinger, Figma Make, Replit. This is currently Remixer's position and it is indefensible in the field.

avoid.pattern: Credit expiry clocks and forfeiture on cancellation
avoid.why: Lovable's pricing FAQ carries three separate defensive questions — 'Do credits expire?', 'What happens to my credits if my subscription ends?', 'Are credits refundable?' — questions that exist because the answers are unpopular. A Trustpilot reviewer: 'The subscription is basically extortion. If you do not use your tokens and end the subscription, they are gone.' Base44: 'Unused credits do not carry over.' Figma: no rollover. v0: 65-day expiry. The expiry clock buys revenue recognition and buys resentment at a very poor exchange rate.

avoid.pattern: Stating in documentation that AI mistakes are non-refundable
avoid.why: Base44 writes it out: 'Credits are non-refundable for tool behavior and AI mistakes. Each prompt still requires work.' Paired with widely reported retry loops — 'The AI sometimes gets stuck on a feature, retries multiple times, and burns through credits without making progress' — this is the most inflammatory sentence in its docs. Bolt's equivalent is 'Bolt subscriptions are non-refundable, as stated in our Terms of Service.' v0's FAQ answers 'Why do v0 agents keep failing and consuming my credits?' with a request for feedback and no policy at all. Writing the refusal down converts a billing quirk into a stated stance users quote back at you.

avoid.pattern: Hiding the credit balance on a separate page
avoid.why: GoDaddy requires User menu → 'Manage my plan' → 'Total AI Credit Usage'. A 2026 hands-on: 'unlike other AI builders that display a running tally of your AI credit use somewhere on the dashboard, GoDaddy keeps Airo's tucked away on a separate screen' — described as 'a nuisance' and listed among the top complaints. Remixer's persistent toolbar chip is already correct; the mistake to avoid is ever demoting it into a settings page.

avoid.pattern: Exposing raw tokens whose cost scales with project size rather than user intent
avoid.why: Bolt's own FAQ concedes it: 'Most token usage is related to syncing your project's file system to the AI: the larger the project, the more tokens used per message.' The consequence is that a 'change the button colour' prompt on a mature project can cost more than a whole feature on a new one — cost becomes uncorrelated with perceived value, which is the definition of an unfair meter. v0 makes the same bet with a 40x output-price spread across models and v0 Max preselected by default. Both sit near the bottom of category sentiment.

avoid.pattern: Decoy headline pricing with the real ladder hidden behind signup
avoid.why: bolt.new/pricing advertises Pro at '$25 per month' with the hedge 'Start at 10M tokens per month', while the billing docs reference Pro 50 at $50/mo, Pro 100 at $100/mo and Pro 200 at $200/mo — none of which appear on the public pricing page. The advertised price anchors acquisition while heavy users land at 2–8x it. Base44 did the adjacent version: post-acquisition price increases and reduced credit allowances discovered by users at billing time with no announcement, plus a Product Hunt reviewer noting 'Seems the price has gone up since acquired by Wix.'

avoid.pattern: Charging more for the same credit capacity to gate governance
avoid.why: Lovable's pricing page shows Pro at $25 with '100 monthly credits' and Business at $50 with '100 monthly credits' — 2x price, identical throughput — and the FAQ carries a dedicated defensive entry, 'Why is the Business plan more expensive?'. A team that needs SSO or role-based access pays double for the same work. If Remixer adds team tiers, the price step should buy capacity as well as controls, or the FAQ writes itself.

avoid.pattern: Publishing a thrift manual instead of fixing the meter
avoid.why: Bolt maintains a documented strategy guide teaching users to avoid its own billing: 'Plan mode uses fewer tokens', 'Use Version History to undo changes without tokens', 'Clear context', 'Turn on connectors only when you need them', 'Reduce the size of your project by removing unused files', 'Avoid repeated automated error fix attempts'. GoDaddy's prompt guide does the same framing: 'Fix my site costs more credits than "The checkout button isn't processing payments..."'. Naming which actions are free is good; needing a manual for not spending money is an admission the model is hostile, and it keeps the meter permanently in the user's foreground.

avoid.pattern: Runtime credits consumed by the end user, which pause features in the live app
avoid.why: Base44's integration credits are a shared workspace pool burned by your customers — email 1, image generation 1, LLM call 1–15, in-app agent messages 3–40 — and exhaustion 'cancels in-progress runs'. Third-party analysis reports mid-month feature pausing for emails, AI calls and automations 'affects the live production app, not just development'. Lovable's version is nearly as bad: at zero credits 'built-in backend services will pause'. The customer hits the paywall instead of the builder — the harshest placement available.

avoid.pattern: Paywalling the escape hatch so cheap tiers must spend credits on trivial changes
avoid.why: Hostinger gates the code editor at Hobbyist ($39.99/mo), so on Explorer ($6.99, 30 credits) and Starter ($13.99, 70 credits) 'you can't touch the generated code. Every change goes through the AI, which means every change costs a credit.' Reviewers recommend the $39.99 tier specifically because 'the code editor access changes the economics: you stop burning credits on small CSS tweaks.' A paywall that makes the cheap tiers structurally more expensive to use converts price-sensitive users into churn rather than upgrades.

avoid.pattern: A free tier that can build but cannot publish
avoid.why: GoDaddy's free tier gives unlimited app creation and 50 credits but 'can only build, not publish' — so the free user hits a wall rather than a pitch, having invested the entire build effort before discovering they own nothing shippable. Replit takes the better line, letting free Starter 'publish up to 1 project' including private/password-protected. Remixer's placement — free staging publish, paid custom domain — is better than GoDaddy's and should be defended, not drifted away from.

avoid.pattern: Daily sub-caps that make a single working session impossible
avoid.why: Base44 Free is capped at 5 credits per DAY (25/month), and a Product Hunt reviewer: 'you'll burn through them just tweaking UI.' Bolt's free 300K/day 'often runs out before a first build finishes' against a documented ~5-minute first build. v0 stacks two independent ceilings: $5 of credits AND 7 messages/day. A daily cap below the cost of one meaningful session doesn't ration usage, it prevents evaluation.

avoid.pattern: Enforcing caps retroactively on existing users
avoid.why: Figma began enforcing Full-seat AI credit limits on 18 March 2026 (3,000/mo Professional). Forum posts record a user's usage collapsing from ~200,000 credits/month to 3,000 — a 98.5% reduction — a $200+ overage month on a single project inside base credits, and a thread arguing extra credits are 5.6x more expensive than simply adding a seat. Thread titles include 'Figma Make Ai Credit Limits Not Feasible' and 'Complaints about AI credit usage'. Whatever Remixer's expiry and cap policy becomes, it must be set before scale, not tightened after.

avoid.pattern: Destructive undo that refunds nothing
avoid.why: Hostinger's Undo 'permanently deletes' the last message and response; Restore confirms 'All your messages after this message will be permanently deleted'; and docs state 'Undoing or restoring a version does not cost additional credits and does not reinstate credits spent on the reverted messages.' Honest, but it means a user who spends 40 credits on a change they immediately reject is 40 credits poorer with nothing to show and no history left. Free restores are correct; a linear destructive history is not.

leapfrog.idea: Pre-flight cost estimate on the Send button, plus a per-project spend cap
leapfrog.spec: As the user types, the Send button grows a live estimate chip reading '~12 credits'. Hovering shows a one-line basis: 'Estimate from 4 files and 1 image. You're only charged for what actually runs.' In Project settings, a 'Spend cap' control: 'Ask me before any single message costs more than [50] credits' (default on, default 50). When the classifier buckets a request above the cap, the composer shows an inline confirm instead of sending: 'This looks like a big change — around 78 credits. [Run it] [Plan it first — 1 credit]'. If actual spend exceeds the estimate by more than 25%, the difference is not charged and the receipt reads 'Cost: 50 credits (estimated 40 — we capped it).'
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Exact token cost is genuinely unpredictable before the agent explores the project, and vendors benefit from the opacity — so the whole field settles for after-the-fact disclosure at best. Lovable shows cost only afterwards in a three-dot menu; Bolt's reviewers name the gap directly ('it is not always clear what a given action will cost before you run it'); GoDaddy publishes no per-action costs at all. But precision isn't required — Base44 already publishes a coarse four-bucket table (0.5 simple / ~1 small feature / ~2 complex module / 3–4 app-wide) and Framer publishes a five-item price list. A classifier that buckets the request plus a cap is sufficient, and the honest failure mode (we eat the overage) is what nobody will commit to.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: We can afford to eat estimate variance because the meter is not where DreamHost's margin lives — hosting, domains and email are. A pure-play AI builder cannot absorb overage without eating its gross margin; a registrar+host can treat the credit meter as a usage governor rather than a profit centre. This turns the field's single most-cited complaint into our single most defensible claim: the only AI builder that tells you the price before you pay it.

leapfrog.idea: Earn credits by attaching a DreamHost domain and a real mailbox
leapfrog.spec: In the centred domain switcher, a card appears while the project is on a *.remixer.app subdomain: 'Connect a DreamHost domain — +500 credits.' One click if the domain is already in the account (zero DNS work). After connection, a follow-on card: 'Add hello@yourdomain.com — +500 credits. Included in your plan.' Earned credits appear in the credits popover as a distinct non-expiring bucket labelled 'Earned' beneath 'Monthly' and 'Daily'. The pricing page carries the line: 'Connect a domain and a mailbox and you've earned back your first two months of credits.'
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Nobody else can. Lovable is a registrar but its docs state plainly it does not provide mailboxes. Bolt sells domains and its entire domains documentation set — connect, purchase, aliases, dns-records, ssl-https — never mentions mailboxes at all. Base44 states 'Custom email domains are for sending only.' v0 sells domains through Vercel but has no email product at any tier. GoDaddy resells Microsoft 365 at $7.99/mo and Hostinger ladders mailboxes 1/2/5 as paid inventory — both monetise email, but neither has thought to spend credits to buy an attach.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: We operate our own registrar, our own hosting and our own mail platform. Every competitor's credit balance only goes down; ours can go up, and it goes up precisely when the customer does the thing that makes DreamHost money and makes them structurally sticky. It also inverts the emotional register of the meter — from a tax on working to a reward for committing — and it uses credits, which cost us compute, to buy domain and email revenue, which is a far better trade than selling the credits.

leapfrog.idea: Automatic credit refunds when our agent regresses the site, with a visible ledger
leapfrog.spec: After every generation, run a build check plus a visual diff against the previous version. On detected regression, the chat posts: 'That change broke your contact form. We've reverted it and refunded 14 credits.' The credits popover gains a fourth line: 'Refunded this month: +42' with a 'Why?' link opening a ledger of timestamped entries — date, what broke, credits returned. Pricing FAQ question: 'What if the AI makes a mistake?' Answer: 'We refund the credits. You should never pay us to fix our own error.'
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: The whole field has taken the opposite position in writing. Base44: 'Credits are non-refundable for tool behavior and AI mistakes.' Bolt: 'subscriptions are non-refundable.' v0's FAQ meets 'Why do v0 agents keep failing and consuming my credits?' with a request for feedback and no policy. Lovable gets closest — fixes are free within fair use — but never returns spend. Detection is the stated obstacle, and it has already been solved in public: v0 loads a headless browser, screenshots its own page and posts desktop and mobile renders back into the chat; Replit Agent 3 runs a visible in-pane browser and you watch its cursor click through the app. The mechanism exists; the willingness to pay for its findings does not.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: Same economics as the estimate: credits are a governor, not our margin, so a refund costs us compute rather than revenue. And it converts the category's loudest, best-documented complaint — third-party analysis frames it exactly as 'every bug the AI introduces is a future credit charge for the user to fix, not for the platform to prevent' — into a single sentence no competitor can currently say back to us.

leapfrog.idea: Credits live in the DreamHost account wallet: they never expire and they survive cancellation
leapfrog.spec: Move credits out of a per-plan bucket into the existing DreamHost account balance. Pricing FAQ: 'Do credits expire?' → 'No. They're yours.' And 'What happens if I cancel?' → 'Your credits stay in your DreamHost account. Come back any time and they're waiting.' In the credits popover, monthly grant and purchased credits are shown as separate lines with purchased credits carrying a small infinity glyph and the tooltip 'Never expires'. Allow purchased credits to be spent against a domain renewal or a mailbox at a published conversion rate.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Expiry is the category's standard churn-suppression and revenue-recognition device, and every player uses it: Lovable expires monthly credits 2 months after issue and annual credits 1 month after the period ends; v0 expires rollover at 65 days; Base44 and Figma have no rollover at all; Framer's free daily grant dies nightly. It is also the source of the sharpest language anyone has written about these products — 'The subscription is basically extortion. If you do not use your tokens and end the subscription, they are gone.' Startups burning venture money on inference cannot afford an open-ended liability.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: DreamHost already runs long-lived account balances for domain renewals and hosting — the wallet is built and the accounting is solved. A host with multi-year customer relationships does not need a 65-day forfeiture clock, and letting credits convert toward a renewal makes the liability productive rather than dead. This is a promise no venture-funded pure-play can match without changing its unit economics.

leapfrog.idea: Make 'the meter never touches your live site' an explicit, contractual guarantee
leapfrog.spec: A guarantee stated in the out-of-credits blocking dialog, the pricing page and the docs: 'Running out of credits never affects your published site. Your pages, forms, database, user accounts, payments and email keep working. Only building pauses.' On the pricing page, a labelled comparison row: 'What breaks when you run out of credits?' — Remixer: 'Nothing that's live.' Add a small persistent status line in the credits popover at zero balance: 'yoursite.com — live and serving' with a green dot.
leapfrog.why_nobody_does_it: Because their architecture makes it untrue. Lovable's docs state that at zero credits 'built-in backend services will pause' — database, storage and authentication become inaccessible while only static pages keep serving, so a live customer-facing app can break because the owner ran out of BUILD credits. Base44 is worse: integration credits are a shared workspace pool consumed by the app's own end users, so a successful launch drains the balance and pauses live email, AI calls and automations mid-month. Emergent charges 50 credits/month simply to keep a deployment alive. In each case the runtime is rented and metered, so the vendor cannot promise it stays up.
leapfrog.remixer_advantage: We own the hosting, the CDN (SmartEdge, 10 PoPs), the SSL and the mail platform, and they are already included in the $9.99 plan rather than drawn from the credit pool. The guarantee costs us nothing to make and is impossible for Lovable, Base44 or Emergent to match without re-architecting. It is also the perfect complement to free publishing: together they say the credit meter governs how fast you build, and never whether your business is online.

open_questions: What does one Remixer credit actually buy? 1,000 credits at $9.99 and Lovable's 100 at $25 are not comparable units, and the top-up maths implies a Remixer credit is roughly 1/20th of a Lovable credit ($0.015 vs $0.30). Until we publish a per-action table in the Framer/Base44 style, '1,000 credits' is a headline number users cannot reason about — and it will produce disappointment on first contact rather than confidence.

Do Remixer credits roll over, and do they expire? The brief does not say. This is the single largest rage generator in the category (Lovable carries three defensive FAQ entries and a 'basically extortion' Trustpilot review) and we currently have no documented position at all.

What is our spend order? This matters immediately because of the 1,000 first-month bonus credits — users must be told whether bonus, monthly or purchased credits are consumed first. GoDaddy and Lovable both use an expiry-first rule; neither surfaces it prominently, so stating it well is cheap differentiation.

What exactly survives a zero balance? Do published pages keep serving, do forms still write to the database, do user accounts still authenticate, do Stripe payments still process, does email still send? If everything stays up, that is a headline claim Lovable and Base44 cannot make and it belongs in the blocking dialog copy.

Is the publish charge flat or proportional to change size? If flat, removing it is a straightforward billing change. If it is proportional — i.e. publishing re-runs generation work — then the coupling is architectural and the fix needs engineering scoping before we can promise free publishing publicly.

Why does the top-up ladder carry a 50% premium over the included rate ($0.015 vs $0.00999 per credit), and why is the 2,500 pack only ~6.7% cheaper per credit than the 1,000 pack? Lovable's premium is ~20%. A weak volume curve punishes exactly the heavy users we most want to keep.

Is the 30-day no-card trial converting better than a perpetual free tier with a daily grant would? The field has moved decisively to perpetual free (Lovable, Bolt, Base44, v0, GoDaddy). Our trial is the longest no-card offer in the category but it is a cliff — we need the day-31 return-rate data before deciding whether it is an asset or a leak.

Where exactly does our paywall sit for staging? If publishing to a *.remixer.app subdomain is free during and after trial, that is materially better than GoDaddy's free tier (which cannot publish at all) and we are not currently claiming it anywhere in our pricing copy.

Are credits pooled per account or per project, and once teams exist, can one member drain the pool? Base44 pools per workspace with no guardrail; Lovable ships per-member credit limits on Pro and a 'credits ping' to owners. We need a position before the first team lands, not after.

What do AI image and asset generation cost, and are they metered separately? Base44 charges 1 integration credit per image and 5 per second of video; Bolt gates image generation behind a manual opt-in toggle in account settings. If Remixer generates imagery inline, that cost needs to appear in the per-action table or it will be the first surprise on a user's receipt.

Do we have telemetry on what share of credits users spend fixing our agent's own errors? Third-party analysis of the category puts typical production-ready landing pages at 150–250 credits against a 30–80 first pass, implying most spend is correction. Without our own number we cannot size the cost of the free-fix policy or the automatic-refund leapfrog.

executive_take:
The category has converged on one answer to "why does that feel expensive," and it is not taste — it is five measurable decisions. (1) A UI typeface nobody else has: Lovable self-hosts Camera Plain Variable 100–900 and exploits intermediate axis values (prices render at weight 480); v0 has Geist; Base44 runs Wix Madefor + Dazzed + Azeret Mono; GoDaddy commissioned GD Sherpa/GD Sage. Bolt is the only major on Inter — and Bolt reads cheapest. (2) A perceptual colour system where only the neutral ramp changes between themes: Lovable's six semantic hues are byte-identical in light and dark, with translucency shifting .16→.2, which is why it looks like one brand in both. (3) Elevation published as a ladder, not a hex — Lovable's dark runs six surfaces ~2.5% lightness apart (20.42/23/24.74/27.2/30/32.8%); Bolt four (#111114/#171719/#1E1E21/#2C2C30); Base44 keeps two neutral ramps and uses the WARM one (stone #f8f6f4→#1b1a19) for every surface, reserving cold grey for disabled states only. (4) Shadows modelled physically: a six-step ramp with geometrically doubling offsets (1/3/6/12/24px), every layer at 4% black, plus per-button inset bevels (`inset 0 1px 0 0 #fff, inset 0 -1px 0 0 #fffc`) — not the AI-default single shadow at 10%. (5) Motion that never overshoots: 150/200/300ms on decelerating curves (Geist: `--ease-standard cubic-bezier(0.2,0,0,1)`; Lovable measured at cubic-bezier(0.4,0,0.2,1) 150–300ms), with hover and pressed encoded as 8%/16% alpha tokens so every interactive surface responds with identical weight.

Two coherent motion philosophies exist and both read premium: Lovable's branded waiting (~39 named keyframes, a literal double-beat `heartbeat` on the logo, checkmarks drawn via stroke-dashoffset) and Vercel's stated opposite — "Default to stillness. Never add auto-scrolling marquees, simulated typing cursors, or decorative pulsing status indicators." What never reads premium is the middle: unmotivated motion.

The uncomfortable part is where that leaves us. The documented AI-slop fingerprint is "the Inter typeface, an indigo-to-purple gradient, three rounded cards in a row"; Tailwind's creator has publicly apologised for making every button `bg-indigo-500`. Remixer's stated language is Inter, an indigo/purple gradient, a cool-leaning near-black (#18181B is blue-leaning by 3 points), and an action blue (#1587FF) within three points of Bolt's #1488FC. By its own spec, our builder currently wears the costume of the thing it is trying not to generate. The real competitive gap, though, is not chrome — it is that nobody in this field designs the registrar moment, the mailbox, or the hosting-layer error page. Those three surfaces are ours alone.

comparison.approach: OKLCH semantic token system with hue-constant dual theming (only the neutral ramp changes; six semantic hues byte-identical across themes, alpha .16→.2). Proprietary variable typeface Camera Plain Variable 100–900 self-hosted, Roboto Mono for code, weight 480 used for prices. Display type locked to line-height 1.100 and tracking -0.0400em at every size (48/52.8/-1.92, 36/39.6/-1.44, 28/30.8/-1.12); body 16/24. Radius 6/8/10/12/16/24/28/32 + full-round, --radius base 0.5rem. Six-step shadow ramp, hairline ring plus geometrically doubling offsets at 4% black, plus per-semantic inset button bevels. Four easing curves at 100–500ms, nothing overshoots. ~39 named keyframes including heartbeat, loader-sweep, shimmer-gradient, status-dot-ping, checkbox-draw-check. Hero is a live 2400×2420 canvas mesh gradient kept BELOW the type so it never fights contrast.
comparison.notes: The only system in the field where every layer — colour space, type, elevation, motion, waiting — is tokenised and internally consistent. Glow tokens (hover 8%, pressed 16% per semantic) are why every control feels the same weight. One wart: the visual hero 'Build something Lovable' at 48px/600 is not the h1; the actual h1 is 'AI App Builder' at 14px/400 grey.

comparison.approach: True black ground oklch(0 0 0), Geist Sans, body text oklch(0.946 0 0), internal v0-gray token scale. Deliberately small hero: h1 at 32px/600/-1.28px (exactly -0.04em) — restraint rather than volume. Three-radius system mapped to role: 12px containers, 6px controls, full-round chips. Bespoke 16px Geist icons in chrome while shipping lucide-react in generated output. Only saturated colour in the whole UI is the code syntax palette (--sh-class #00a7fd, --sh-string #00e7c1, --sh-keyword #ff0078, --sh-jsxliterals #ffff72). iOS app streams text with a pooled staggered fade capped at 4 concurrent words at 32ms; Liquid Glass composer with progressive blur.
comparison.notes: Geist's published motion guidance is ~150ms state change / 200ms popover / 300ms overlay on cubic-bezier(0.2,0,0,1), and the brand guide bans decorative motion outright. Deductions: builder toolbar icons ship with aria-label and title both null; the preview pane shows only 'Your v0 generation will show here.' for the full 6m21s build; in-app motion beyond the composer is sparse.

comparison.approach: Most mature token system for its age. Two parallel neutral ramps — warm 'stone' (#f8f6f4→#1b1a19) for all surfaces, cool 'neutral' reserved for disabled and dark shimmer. Wix Madefor Text/Display + Dazzed brand + Azeret Mono. Five-step duration scale (80/120/180/260/360ms) and three named easings: --ease-out cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1), --ease-in-out cubic-bezier(.65,0,.35,1), --ease-spring cubic-bezier(.34,1.56,.64,1). Interaction state tokenised as opacity (disabled .4, muted .65, hover .85, press .75, scrim .32) plus a named z-index ladder and per-intent focus rings. Shadows are warm-black (#1c1a18/#0f0e0e) at 5%, plus --shadow-glass-top: inset 0 1px 0 #ffffff80. Radius none/2/4/6/8/12/16/24/32 + card 10 + pill 100; strict 4px spacing grid. Three named themes and a [data-ds=base44] namespace implying a swappable DS.
comparison.notes: Uniquely defines 'premium' as a first-class semantic intent — --sem-fill-premium-* across primary/secondary/light/ghost × default/hover/active/disabled, --focus-ring-premium, --gradient-premium (orange-100→purple-200→purple-300) — so every paywall looks designed rather than bolted on. Deductions: two different design languages (warm-paper Dazzed/Geist marketing vs Wix Madefor editor), and raw Python stack traces ('dict' object has no attribute 'lower') leak to a no-code audience.

comparison.approach: Deliberately refuses to invent an AI chrome — inherits Figma Design's right rail, presents the DOM as 'layers view for code', adds device-frame previews inside the editing loop. Toolbar splits 'Edit' and 'Annotate for agent'. Numbered blue on-canvas callouts carry intent-level and now motion-level instructions; Figma's own examples include 'fade this button in after a 300ms delay' and 'add a subtle press effect when this button is tapped'. Publish modal carries a Typography alert for missing WOFF/WOFF2 web fonts before go-live.
comparison.notes: Highest craft-per-decision in the sweep even though it has no distinct visual identity of its own — that's the strategy. The staged, credit-free direct-manipulation model ('Edits stack up in the chat panel first, staged and credit-free, until you apply them') is the single best pricing-meets-design mechanism in the category. Deduction: no real version history in Make files.

comparison.approach: Full dark token set: brand #1488FC (hover #2BA6FF), surfaces #111114/#171719/#1E1E21/#2C2C30, text #F9F6F9/#D6D5DE/#A4A3AC, semantics each with a matching *BgSubtle at 1a alpha. Inter + Inter Display with --font-settings 'cv01','ss03' and opsz auto; h1 48px/48px (1.0 ratio)/700/-1.2px. Bimodal radius with a real rule: 6px chrome, 8px base, full pills reserved for AI-facing controls (Plan toggle, Build now, import chips). Terminal themed with the Hyper Snazzy palette rather than xterm defaults. Loading is a five-stop specular sweep token (#0a0a0a→#2ba6ff 21.5%→#fff 33%→#2ba6ff 65.5%→#0a0a0a) plus rgba(255,255,255,.06) skeleton shimmer and a text-shimmer for 'thinking' prose. Motion is one curve, one duration: 0.15s cubic-bezier(0.4,0,0.2,1), enumerated per property.
comparison.notes: The pill-means-AI radius rule and the branded loading bar are both directly stealable. But Inter is the named slop typeface, there is no light theme, and the brand blue sits within three points of ours — meaning Bolt is currently the reason our accent reads as category-default rather than proprietary. Shipped marketing copy contains real punctuation errors ('interface no extra accounts'), which undercuts the premium read.

comparison.approach: Best single composition in the field: near-black violet ground (~#150A1F–#1B0D2B), headline alternating white and violet (~#8B5CF6) per phrase, and a pure-white full-radius prompt pill floating inside a multi-layer lavender bloom — the halo, not a border, does the work. Proprietary GD Sherpa (UI) + GD Sage (editorial serif). Violet is reserved with real discipline: BETA pill, alternating headline words, prompt glow, send buttons, AI sparkle — every non-AI control is neutral. Radii are bimodal by mode: full pill on marketing/AI surfaces, ~8–12px on working chrome. Sibling W+M builder narrates generation with an elapsed counter ('Worked for 45s') and names design decisions in plain language ('Applied gelato color theme — Paired with bubblegum fonts.').
comparison.notes: Then it breaks its own spell: the dark violet entry screen gives way to a light builder interior, so the product you fell for is not the product you use. No documented motion values anywhere. Two names for one control across docs ('Preview Desktop' vs 'Change device'), Menu and Media as two separate asset surfaces, and help pages wrapped in the commercial mega-nav. Note the exact hex values are estimated from GoDaddy's own screenshots, not measured.

comparison.approach: Functional IDE visual language with strong choreography rather than strong tokens. Agent 3's App Testing opens a real browser inside the Agent pane and renders the agent's own cursor clicking through the app it just built. Agent 4 replaced the Design Mode tab with an infinite 'Design Canvas' and moved collaboration to a shared Kanban (Drafts/Active/Ready/Done). Element Editor is a click-to-edit overlay covering text, size, weight, alignment, colour, margin and padding.
comparison.notes: No published token evidence for colour, type, radius, shadow or easing — the craft is entirely in motion and choreography. The visible agent cursor is the most legible generation state anyone has shipped and is a motion-design decision as much as a feature.

comparison.approach: Keeps the AI inside an established design-tool canvas rather than giving it its own chrome — layers, frames, auto-layout and visual breakpoints all behave as expected, with Wireframer and Workshop layered in as prompt surfaces. Publishes per-action credit costs (landing page ~300, responsive layout 150, large edit 100, small edit 50) with model multipliers.
comparison.notes: Scored on inherited canvas credibility, not on independently verified tokens — specific typefaces, hex values, radii and easing could not be verified without logging in, so treat any token-level claim as unsourced. The strategic lesson is the same as Figma Make's: refusing to invent an AI aesthetic lets the AI inherit the tool's existing authority.

comparison.approach: Undistinguished studio chrome, but ships the strongest design-QUALITY mechanism in the sweep: 'Design Variations' generates five complete alternative directions — distinct layouts, colour approaches and typographic choices — from one click, previewable and applyable without re-prompting. Plus canvas annotation directly on the running app ('Draw on your app, tweak components and generate new visuals') and inline image generation via Nano Banana.
comparison.notes: Proof that the anti-generic problem is solvable with a button rather than a better prompt. Free, which sets a difficult price expectation. The chrome itself contributes nothing to the premium question.
